items.body:
Myprotein, the UK’s leading sports brand, has today announced the launch of its Lift Seamless collection, strengthening the brand’s women’s activewear portfolio with performance-led styles designed around strength training.The collection combines soft-touch seamless fabrication with targeted design details, flattering silhouettes and bold colourways, with the range designed to support women who lift and provide flexibility, comfort and unrestricted movement during training.
The Lift Seamless collection combines soft-touch, four-way stretch seamless fabrication with sweat-wicking, quick-drying and antimicrobial finishing. Glute-enhancing textures and signature scrunch detailing feature across key styles, designed to separate and enhance the glutes while creating a flattering silhouette.
The launch introduces three new styles: the Lift Bandeau Bra, Lift Seamless Shrug and Lift Body Fit Seamless T-Shirt, expanding the range with additional silhouettes for strength training and beyond.
Designed with a minimal, body-fit silhouette, the Lift Seamless Shrug features a super open back, bolero front, long sleeves and thumbholes. Made from soft-touch seamless fabric, the shrug features sweat-wicking, quick-drying and antimicrobial finishing.
Commenting on the launch, Joseph Duffill, MP Activewear Womenswear Designer, said: “The Lift Seamless collection has been designed specifically with women who lift in mind. Whether it’s for a dedicated strength session, a full-body gym workout, a warm-up or cool-down, we wanted to create pieces that offer the comfort, flexibility and performance.
We’re also seeing the way women wear activewear continue to change, with pieces increasingly moving beyond the gym into everyday life. From travelling to and from the gym and grabbing a coffee after a workout, to layering pieces for the rest of the day, the collection is designed to offer the versatility women are looking for, combining technical fabrications with flattering silhouettes and carefully chosen details.”
Alongside the new additions, the wider Lift Seamless collection includes the Lift Seamless Legging, Lift Seamless Shorts and Lift Strappy Back Bra. The wider She Lifts offering also includes the Tempo Good Seamless Halter Neck Vest, Tempo Good Seamless Flare Legging, Tempo Zip Through Hoodie and Tempo Mid-Rise Straight Leg Jogger.
The full Myprotein Lift Seamless collection is available from the 14th of September at myprotein.com with all sizes available in sizes XS–XXL.

items.title: Retailers risk trading pounds in parcel claims for pennies off delivery rates this peak
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Analysis from the UK’s most successful AI-powered courier claims platform Claimit has found that the value of retaining courier claims rights significantly outweighs small savings on parcel delivery rates, particularly during the peak trading period. A reduction of five pence per parcel would save £5,000 across 100,000 deliveries. However, Claimit’s analysis during last year’s peak […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Analysis from the UK’s most successful AI-powered courier claims platform Claimit has found that the value of retaining courier claims rights significantly outweighs small savings on parcel delivery rates, particularly during the peak trading period.
A reduction of five pence per parcel would save £5,000 across 100,000 deliveries. However, Claimit’s analysis during last year’s peak period found that 1.5% of parcels shipped generated a claim, while parcel volumes increased 2.5 times compared with off-peak. With courier payouts capped as low as £25 per parcel, those claims could represent up to £37,500 in potential compensation, more than 7 times the savings made on the delivery rate.
Parcel volumes also increased 2.5 times compared with off-peak, further increasing the value at stake. Claimit says this underlines why retailers should scrutinise delivery agreements that offer a cheaper headline rate while restricting the ability to claim when something goes wrong.
Courier liability caps mean retailers recover only a fraction of the retail value associated with a lost parcel delivery. In one example, Claimit recovered £2.5 million in courier credits over a year, despite the parcels involved representing £16 million in retail value. The credits recovered were equivalent to less than 16% of that value, demonstrating how much exposure can remain with the retailer even when eligible claims are successfully pursued.
Andy Watson, co-founder of Claimit, says: “Retailers are under enormous pressure to take cost out of every parcel, so shaving a few pence off the delivery rate can understandably look attractive. But the cost of delivery is only one part of the process of getting an order to a customer. Even when retailers retain their claims rights, liability caps mean the credit they receive can be only a fraction of the retail value that has disappeared from the business. That makes those claims rights valuable. If you then give up the ability to recover £20 or £25 when something goes wrong in exchange for saving two, three or five pence on every delivery, that saving can very quickly become a false economy.”
Claims allow retailers to recoup part of the cost when deliveries fail and provide a financial mechanism for holding carriers accountable for service failures. Claimit has found that automation can increase claim success from 13% to over 70% and cut manual processing time by as much as 80%.
Watson added, “Peak is when that trade-off matters most. Volumes increase sharply, more parcels generate claims and suddenly the impact of a seemingly small contractual decision is being multiplied across hundreds of thousands or millions of deliveries. Retailers need to understand how much of the financial risk they are agreeing to carry when a parcel doesn’t arrive as expected.”
Claimit automates the process of claiming for lost and damaged items, connecting directly with retailers’ CRM and ecommerce systems. The platform gives retailers real-time visibility over lost and damaged parcels and invoicing errors, helping them recover revenue without adding to the administrative burden on customer service, operations or logistics teams.
Claimit is the first dedicated courier claims platform and is used by hundreds of retail brands to identify and recover money owed on lost, damaged and incorrectly invoiced parcels. As retailers look for ways to protect margins during peak, recovering revenue already owed to the business should be considered alongside efforts to reduce fulfillment costs.

items.title: Family-run home retailer doubles warehouse footprint after record year
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Leeds-based bathroom retailer Sanctuary Bathrooms is more than doubling its warehouse footprint after a record year for online revenue, leasing a new 16,353sq ft warehouse in Holbeck as it invests in fulfilment capacity, its product range, and its team. The family-run retailer, which supplies homeowners and trade customers across the UK with high-quality, competitively priced […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Leeds-based bathroom retailer Sanctuary Bathrooms is more than doubling its warehouse footprint after a record year for online revenue, leasing a new 16,353sq ft warehouse in Holbeck as it invests in fulfilment capacity, its product range, and its team.
The family-run retailer, which supplies homeowners and trade customers across the UK with high-quality, competitively priced bathroom fixtures, fittings, and accessories, secured the lease on the additional Holbeck unit in August 2026. The new site adds to its existing 12,000sq ft warehouse operation, taking Sanctuary Bathrooms’ total warehouse footprint beyond 28,000sq ft.
The investment follows strong growth across Sanctuary Bathrooms’ ecommerce operation, with online revenue and transactions both increasing at double-digit rates between 2024 and 2025, and 2025 marking a record year for online revenue, despite subdued conditions in the wider bathroom retail market. Website sessions and page views also rose by more than 20% over the same period. That momentum has continued in 2026, with both metrics up more than 15% year to date compared with the equivalent period in 2025, according to GA4 data.
The additional space will allow Sanctuary Bathrooms to hold more stock on site and reduce its reliance on external storage during peak trading periods, while helping the retailer shorten customer lead times and fulfil orders more efficiently.
The increased capacity will also give Sanctuary Bathrooms greater flexibility to broaden and diversify its product range at a time when economic pressures are prompting many manufacturers to streamline their ranges and reduce stockholding. The retailer has continued to expand its offer across different styles and price points in response to customer demand, adding established brands including TOTO in 2025 and Laufen and Imex in 2026.
The additional space will also help strengthen existing supplier relationships, create opportunities to work with new partners, and accelerate plans to expand Sanctuary Bathrooms’ own-brand range with UK and overseas suppliers.
Director James Roberts says: “We have never shied away from investing in our people or the infrastructure needed to grow, and securing this additional warehouse capacity is an important step in scaling the business.
“Customers increasingly expect fast and reliable fulfilment, while retailers also need the resilience to respond to changing trading conditions and pressures across the supply chain. Holding more stock ourselves gives us greater control over availability and the customer experience, while reducing our reliance on external storage.
“It also gives us room to broaden our product offering, develop our own-brand ranges further, and build relationships with new suppliers as we continue to grow.”
The retailer has also made five new hires in 2026, increasing overall headcount by 20%, from 24 to 29. Three of the appointments are in marketing, with two in warehouse operations.
Digital marketing manager Mark Fullilove, who joined Sanctuary Bathrooms in 2020 as its first in-house marketer, says: “When I joined Sanctuary Bathrooms, the ambition was to build on the success of an established family business and accelerate its online growth. To see that strategy translate into sustained growth in both online revenue and transactions is incredibly rewarding.
“That online growth relies on much more than the website itself. From marketing and product choice through to customer service, stock availability, and fulfilment, every part of the customer journey has to work together.
“The additional warehouse capacity and the continued investment we are making in our team give us a strong platform to build on that momentum.”
Among the new hires are Rebecca Parvin-Graham as Digital PR Manager and Halle Audsley as Social Media Manager, marking the first time Sanctuary Bathrooms has brought dedicated PR and social media roles in house. The appointments will strengthen key marketing channels and help build the retailer’s profile and brand awareness in Leeds and across the UK.

items.title: Fed calls for government to put independent retailers at heart of its Budget agenda
items.summary: The national president of the Federation of Independent Retailers (the Fed) Hemanshu Patel has once again called on the government to keep small shops at the heart of its growth agenda in a letter to chancellor John Healey MP in the run up to his… This story continues at Fed calls for government to put independent retailers at heart of its Budget agenda Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Patel’s call came as part of the Fed’s submission ahead of the Budget, which is scheduled for Wednesday, 28 October.
A similar call for action on business rates, rising operating costs, including above inflation increases to the minimum wage, and retail crime was contained in an earlier letter to Healey when he was appointed as chancellor by new prime minister Andy Burnham at the end of July.
Responding to that first letter in August, Healey wrote: “There is a great amount to do during the coming months and I look forward to working with you to achieve our mutual goals.”
Among key concerns raised in Patel’s latest letter are:
- Rogue trade and retail crime rates remain unacceptably high, despite a recent plateauing, with a call for continued investment in neighbourhood policing and ring-fenced resourcing for trading standards teams.
- A call to increase the employer National Insurance Contribution threshold above £5,000 to at least £7,000, as this will particularly help small shops boost employment for those on the margins of employment, such as part-timers and young staff members.
- The impact of business rate increases and losing out on Small Business Rates Relief (SBRR) following the recent April revaluation, with a call on the government to increase the threshold for SBRR from its current base of 100% relief level of £12,000 per annum, to £18,000 or higher.
- Action on energy bills. The Fed’s budget submission also highlights how it is working with Sarah Edwards MP on the Trust and Transparency Charter campaign to create greater competition in the energy market.
Concluding the letter, Patel wrote: “This remains a challenging time for our members and those across the independent convenience sector as they continue to face high taxation and high energy costs.
“Whilst the Fed acknowledges the fiscal challenges the government must deal with, we hope that the needs of small retail businesses – and the wider social and economic benefits they provide – are also factored into the decisions you will need to make in this Budget and beyond.”

items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Retail Insight, the AI-powered retail operations platform trusted by the world’s leading retailers, today announced the launch of DecisionInsight, a new part of its AI-powered retail operations platform that lets retail teams ask a question of their operational data in plain language and get to the cause and the fix in minutes. DecisionInsight is an […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Retail Insight, the AI-powered retail operations platform trusted by the world’s leading retailers, today announced the launch of DecisionInsight, a new part of its AI-powered retail operations platform that lets retail teams ask a question of their operational data in plain language and get to the cause and the fix in minutes.
DecisionInsight is an on-demand AI analytics platform for retail: one place where anyone in a retailer can find insight rooted in the facts of their own operation. Users ask questions in everyday language and get back a written answer, with the numbers behind it visualised in charts that make the story clear at a glance, and a view on what to do next.
It exists because the questions retailers need answered have outpaced the reporting built to answer them. Every function now wants operational answers the same day, customised exactly to them. A report designed to a weekly rhythm was never going to answer something that only occurred to someone this morning, and retail moves faster than that. An experienced senior analyst can spend up to four hours investigating a single performance question whereas DecisionInsight can surface the answer and its drivers in minutes, giving teams time to act before the opportunity is lost.
The strength of the platform comes from what sits underneath it, where DecisionInsight brings together three things: the retailer’s own operational data and the ontology that gives it meaning, the datasets and domain expertise Retail Insight has built over two decades in retail, and the most capable AI models available today. Each of those is valuable in its own right, but it is the combination that makes the difference, with the AI bringing the speed, the ontology meaning the platform reads the business the way the business defines itself, and two decades in retail turning a fast answer into a relevant, accurate and actionable one.
In practice that means bringing together core operational retail data, spanning sales, deliveries, promotions, on-shelf availability, inventory, waste and markdowns, labour, forecasting, weather and supplier performance, and letting anyone question all of it without needing to know where any of it lives or how to build the analysis. It does not stop at what happened either, because the platform will identify the root cause of a problem and recommend the next best actions to take.
“Retailers have no shortage of data. The difficulty has always been getting to answers quickly enough to act on them,” said Alex Considine Tong, Chief Product Officer at Retail Insight. “AI can analyse vast volumes of information at extraordinary speed, but without context and a deep understanding of that data, it can just as easily lead you to the wrong conclusion. Very few companies can bring the context and the technology to the same problem, and twenty years in retail technology and data is what lets us do it.”
DecisionInsight’s context comes from a semantic model that understands the retailer’s own business, and it is the reason every answer can show its working: users can follow the reasoning as the platform goes, see what is established fact and what has been inferred, and trace any figure back to the analysis that produced it. Answers also arrive framed for whoever is asking, with purpose-built agents for category owners, senior leadership, supply chain, store operations leads and store managers, none of which leave the user to work out for themselves what to do about it.
Once a team trusts an answer, the platform can act on it, running the analysis to a schedule and sending it out automatically to the people who need to see it, whether that is a category team receiving a weekly read on their own performance or a supplier receiving a performance scorecard, so the work of chasing down an issue and getting it in front of the right person happens without anyone having to remember to do it.
“What excites us is how ordinary this makes it feel,” said Considine Tong. “A store manager, a category owner and a director can all ask the same question in their own words and get an answer they can act on before the day is out. That is a very different way of working with retail data, and it allows retailers’ analytics teams to operate where they belong, on the problems only they can solve.”
DecisionInsight is available as a web application, as a mobile app, and as an integration for retailers running their own AI agents, who can connect it through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and have it answer questions from inside the tools their teams already use.

items.title: Jigsaw reports an 18% year-on-year increase in sales for Spring/Summer 2026
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. British fashion brand Jigsaw reports an 18% year-on-year increase in sales for Spring/Summer 2026, continuing the momentum established over Christmas 2025 and providing further support to last year’s strategic reset. The performance was delivered against a subdued market backdrop. BRC-KPMG Retail Sales Monitor latest data says non-food retail sales were broadly flat across the season, […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
British fashion brand Jigsaw reports an 18% year-on-year increase in sales for Spring/Summer 2026, continuing the momentum established over Christmas 2025 and providing further support to last year’s strategic reset.
The performance was delivered against a subdued market backdrop. BRC-KPMG Retail Sales Monitor latest data says non-food retail sales were broadly flat across the season, with total sales falling 3% in April. Retailers are also absorbing higher employment costs and business rates, with little targeted support for business ahead of the Autumn Budget.
Against this backdrop, customers continued to prioritise Jigsaw, with growth across every channel. Online sales increased 21%, including 19% in the UK and 48% internationally. Concession sales rose 47%, while store sales increased 6% overall and 11% like-for-like.
The result reflects Jigsaw’s renewed focus on product quality that defines the brand in its new era: distinctive design, quality fabrics, fit and elevated, wearable British fashion. Under its new leadership team, this stronger product focus has been combined with greater commercial discipline across buying, stock management and full-price trading.
Strong product led the season. Dresses grew 43%, led by occasion wear and print, alongside strong performance in jersey. Customers increasingly bought across categories to create complete looks, with cover-ups selling particularly strongly alongside dresses. Jigsaw’s yellow suit, launched in March, sold out within three weeks.
The business has also strengthened its operating platform, transitioning seamlessly to third-party logistics provider Torque, and returning to its refurbished headquarters at Kew Studios.
With the turnaround increasingly established at home, Jigsaw is beginning the next phase of its growth strategy, including selectively expanding its international reach. This Autumn/Winter it will launch through the Nordstrom and Macy’s marketplaces in partnership with Refined Networks, giving the brand access to a significantly broader US customer base.
The performance follows Jigsaw’s strategic reset in 2025, which installed a refreshed team led by Tikki Godley as Managing Director. The strategy has focused on strengthening the core UK business, restoring authority and consistency to the product offer and creating a scalable platform from which the brand can grow across channels and geographies.
Tikki Godley, Managing Director of Jigsaw, said: “This season is further evidence that our turnaround is working. Customers are watching their wallets right now, but still choosing Jigsaw. We have focused relentlessly on making the product better and more distinctive, while bringing greater discipline to how we buy, trade and operate. Customers are responding, and importantly we are seeing that across stores, digital and concessions
David Ross said: “I would like to thank every single one of our employees in the stores, studio, and our suppliers, who work day in and out to exceed customer expectations and deliver our exceptional product to the shelves seamlessly. The AW26 is coming to stores and is one of our best yet. I can’t wait for our customers to see it.”

items.title: JW Filshill posts robust results amid challenging market conditions
items.summary: JW Filshill, which supplies KeyStore convenience stores and independent retailers across Scotland and the north of England, saw turnover remain robust – in line with the overall market trend – at £213m for the year ending 31 January 2026. Amid ongoing challenging market conditions, the… This story continues at JW Filshill posts robust results amid challenging market conditions Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Amid ongoing challenging market conditions, the fifth-generation business, based at Westway Park near Glasgow Airport, saw operating profit slightly down at £4.1m against £5.0m the previous year, the drop of £0.9m due to increases in employers’ national insurance contributions and the minimum wage.
The company also invested heavily in product development relating to its growing Eldorado Tonic Wine brand.
However, profit before tax increased 72% from £4.9m to £8.4m, primarily due to the revaluation of its investment properties, in particular its former headquarters at Ainslie Avenue, Hillington, from where the business relocated in 2023.
Filshill, which also specialises in brand ownership and development, said it has continued to deliver against a clearly defined corporate strategy and ambitions for the future, as well as driving efficiency across the business.
Keith Geddes, chief financial and operating officer, said: “We have continued to deliver against our clearly defined corporate strategy and ambitions and drive efficiency throughout our operation. This improved efficiency is more essential than ever given the increase in costs driven mainly by changes to fuel, living wage and employers’ national insurance costs.
“The directors are pleased with the company performance and are confident that profits will continue at a satisfactory level going forward.
“The long-term success of the company is central to everything we do. We invest heavily in long-term return projects to protect future revenue streams. This includes constantly updating our technology, equipment, and vehicle fleet on an ongoing basis – an approach that has resulted in greater efficiencies and customer satisfaction.”
Noting that Filshill continued to invest heavily in upskilling its employees to take full advantage of advancements in artificial intelligence, he said: “We will ensure that we make use of these tools across all areas of the business.
“We also continue to push forward with investment in other areas of technology such as the innovative use of data, Scope 3 emissions tracking software and industry-specific opportunities for our KeyStore customers in relation to, for example, electronic shelf-edge labels.”
Further discussing the company’s environmental commitments, Geddes said: “During the year, our environmental team has continued working to reduce our carbon footprint and identify areas where we can positively influence a reduction in our carbon impact and work towards a net-zero emissions position.
“We have continued to incur additional operating cost to use hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) in place of diesel for most of our transport fleet and we have pushed to maximise the use of our electric fleet, and to learn and understand how best to use these vehicles, to further reduce our carbon footprint.
“We continue to engage and collaborate with a number of external bodies (both in the public and private sector) to share ideas and best practice.”
“Our project to benchmark our Scope 3 emissions is ongoing and, while this has been difficult, we have continued to invest much time, effort, and money to do this. We have engaged with trade organisations the Scottish Wholesale Association and Food & Drink Wholesale UK and software suppliers to start to measure the carbon footprint of the thousands of products we buy and sell as well as the impact of packaging and staff travel.”
In an independent retail market that remains highly competitive and challenging, Geddes said the company “seeks to manage the principal risk of losing customers by aiming to deliver best-in-class customer service”, adding that any loss of support from key suppliers in terms of supply or credit is also a key risk.
“To offset this, the group works hard to maintain strong partnership-based relationships with all suppliers and was again recently ranked number one by suppliers in an independent survey (Advantage Group Mirror report) across our key competitors for the 16th consecutive year. “Availability of products remains more challenging than previously experienced, but we work very closely with our supply partners to minimise the challenges this creates.”
Recent inflation and increases in the cost of living, in particular increases in the cost of fuel and food and drink, continue to cause uncertainty for the company, staff, customers and suppliers, Geddes pointed out, adding that legislation in the sector is also an “increasing risk but mitigated by close engagement with industry bodies”.
A long-time supporter of charities and good causes around its headquarters but also individual KeyStore shops across Scotland and the north of England, Filshill regards this support as a key pillar of its company strategy, along with building relationships with staff, customers and suppliers. “We are proud of our contribution to supporting our community,” Geddes added.
“Reputation is particularly important to the directors and all decisions within the business are made within the framework of our key corporate values, and in particular our value of ‘Doing the right thing’.

items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Welcoming unexpected visitors has long been part of British life, but new research from Uber Eats reveals lots of us are scrambling when guests arrive without warning, or avoiding friends and family entirely. Shockingly, a quarter (25%) of adults admit to physically hiding when an unexpected guest knocks, with Gen Z being the biggest culprits […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Welcoming unexpected visitors has long been part of British life, but new research from Uber Eats reveals lots of us are scrambling when guests arrive without warning, or avoiding friends and family entirely. Shockingly, a quarter (25%) of adults admit to physically hiding when an unexpected guest knocks, with Gen Z being the biggest culprits of this (30%).
It seems this anxiety stems largely from hosting unpreparedness. Over half of Brits (56%) feel embarrassed by their snack options when people drop by, 23% doubt their ability to brew a decent cup of tea, and more than a fifth (21%) confess to serving guests expired milk in the hope they wouldn’t notice. Others have attempted to serve a questionable food spread, including stale biscuits (26%) and mismatched fridge meats (21%).
So it’s no surprise that nearly 40% of Brits are desperately seeking to level up their hosting skills. To help tackle this ‘Doorbell Dread’, Tesco and Uber Eats are launching Doorbell Drops – a premium range of half-price hosting essentials delivered to the door in minutes.
According to the research, a hilarious generational double-standard towards spontaneous visits is evolving. Gen Z are actually the biggest culprits for unexpected drop-ins, with a quarter (25.1%) admitting they pop in to see friends and family unannounced two to three times a month. However, it seems they’re not as fond of being on the receiving end, with less than one in ten (6.8%) of Gen Z surveyed saying they’re happy to host last-minute guests. In contrast, 36% of Boomers welcome spontaneous drop-ins, despite being the least likely to arrive unannounced (37% say they would never dream of it!).
To help flustered hosts hold the manners high-ground, etiquette expert William Hanson has backed ordering Tesco on Uber Eats as one of his essential drop-in hosting hacks: “Hosting with elegance shouldn’t require days of preparation,” says Hanson. “The secret to last-minute hospitality isn’t slaving over a stove; it’s seamlessly curating a non-chalant vibe to echo that of your drop-in visitors. Tapping into Uber Eats to get a fresh spread of Tesco Finest products delivered before your guest has even taken off their coat is the ultimate power move for a modern host.”
Hanson’s last-minute hosting hacks:
- Tactically divert your guests’ attention – If a surprise drop-in leaves your living area looking less like a home and more like a pig pen, please ensure you do not profusely apologise. A good host never draws attention to their own shortcomings. Instead, swiftly direct your uninvited guests to a comfortable armchair, pour them a drink, and keep the lighting softly dimmed. Candlelight is wonderfully forgiving of unvacuumed rugs and unmade cushions.
- Stock the emergency larder in a pinch – Panic-hosting requires swift execution, not a panicked dash to a crowded supermarket. If your fridge is currently housing a half empty jar of chutney and a single lime, open the Uber Eats app and tap through to the Tesco hub page. Order from the Doorbell Drops page, stocked with Tesco essentials – crisps, olives, tea and quality biscuits – and delivered straight to your door. Transfer everything onto proper china serving dishes before your guests even notice the doorbell ring. Packaging is for the pantry, not the parlour.
- Master the illusion of preparation – Never let guests see you sweat over a kitchen stove. For last minute visitors, elaborate hot meals are an absolute faux pas – they force you to spend the entire time away from the conversation. Serve ambient, high quality nibbles on elevated platters, or present a well curated charcuterie board. A guest should feel catered to, not like an inconvenience you are actively labouring over.
- Keep the conversation moving – The hallmark of exceptional hosting isn’t a flawless home; it’s making your guests feel utterly at ease. The moment they arrive, place a glass in their hand (always offer a sophisticated non-alcoholic option alongside wine or spirits). As the host, your primary duty is to steer the conversation away from awkward lulls, manage the room’s energy, and ensure no glass remains empty for longer than a couple of minutes.
- Have an elegant ending cue – A gracious host knows how to welcome guests, but a masterful host knows how to usher them out when the evening has run its course. When you are ready to reclaim your evening, do not stand up and awkwardly stretch. Simply offer one final round of water or tea, or ask with polite concern: “Do you have a particularly early start tomorrow?” It is the universal, civilised code for: it is time to put your coat on.
Customers can now visit the Doorbell Drops hub page for Tesco on the Uber Eats app to shop these curated hosting essentials at half-price*, including Tesco Finest All Butter Sultana Scones alongside strawberry jam and clotted cream, Mcvities Chocolate Digestives, Président French Brie with Jacobs crackers and Tesco Green Olives with Slow Roasted Tomatoes.
Merve Basci, Uber Eats UK general manager, said: “Unannounced visits used to be a staple of British social and community life, but the fear of being unprepared and judged for stale biscuits is driving many to hide rather than host. Whether it’s dodging in-laws or frantically scouring the fridge for something edible to serve, our new partnership with Tesco can help people ditch the ‘doorbell dread’, so that young people especially can relax and enter their hosting era with more confidence.”
Suzanne Quinn, Tesco customer director, said: “At Tesco, we’re always looking for little helps that make life easier for customers, and expanding our rapid delivery service through our Uber Eats partnership is another way we’re helping the nation get what they need, when they need it. The Doorbell Deals range has been created for those moments when plans change or guests arrive at short notice, giving customers quick access to fresh food, drink, and hosting essentials, so they can conveniently pull together a delicious spread in minutes.”
This launch follows Tesco’s recent partnership with Uber Eats, extending rapid grocery delivery, Clubcard Prices and Clubcard points to more customers across the UK. The Uber Eats and Tesco Doorbell Drop range will be available at half-price on the Uber Eats app until 20 September.

items.body:
The Australian skincare brand brings its clinically inspired wrinkle solutions to more than 60 Boots stores and boots.com from the 9th September.
The launch marks Wrinkles Schminkles’ first UK retail partnership, bringing its targeted, non-invasive wrinkle patches to a wider UK audience. Having built a loyal DTC following in the UK, the brand is now stepping into physical retail through Boots, one of the most current and coveted launchpads in the market.
Initial store locations include London Tottenham Court Road, Covent Garden, Knightsbridge, Manchester Market Street and dedicated Boots Beauty stores including Battersea and Bristol Cabot Circus.
The international expansion follows Wrinkles Schminkles’ acquisition by Avenir Collective and marks a new phase of growth for the brand, which was founded to transform established silicone technology into simple, targeted skincare for use at home.
“The launch with Boots is a major milestone for Wrinkles Schminkles and an exciting moment as we relaunch globally. There’s a powerful opportunity at the intersection of beauty, aesthetics and at-home care, and we believe Wrinkles Schminkles complements the growing professional skincare market while bringing results-led solutions into everyday beauty routines. Boots offer the perfect launch platform to make that shift, taking a brand with strong category credibility to a much broader beauty audience,” Lauren Myers, chief brand officer at Avenir Collective
Founded in Australia in 2014, Wrinkles Schminkles sits between skincare and the clinic. The brand is most known for pioneering the reusable 100% medical grade silicone patch, designed to support smoother- looking, more hydrated and visibly firmer skin.
Inspired by the established use of medical-grade silicone in scar care, the brand has refined the technology into targeted patches for specific areas including the forehead, eyes, mouth, neck and chest. The brand also leads with ingredient-led SKUs, including Self-Dissolving Microneedle Patches, Face Polishing Peel Pads powered by AHAs, BHAs and PHAs, and Facial Plumping Sheet Masks with peptides, collagen and hyaluronic acid.
The initial Boots assortment includes 10 SKUs, featuring hero products such as the Forehead Wrinkle Patches, Chest Wrinkle Patch and Self-Dissolving Microneedle Patches, alongside the new Brow Frown & Bunny Lines Wrinkle Patches launching in September exclusively to Boots. Each patch is designed to be worn overnight or a few hours for a quick boost, and can be reused multiple times. With each SKU priced between £15–30RRP, Wrinkles Schminkles remains focused on offering an accessible entry point forBoots customers.

items.body:
Asda has become the country’s largest supported internship provider after creating 210 new placement opportunities for young people with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) across 35 stores nationwide.
The expansion means Asda’s supported internship programme now operates in more locations than any other UK business, addressing a significant employment gap facing young people with learning disabilities. Only 4.8% of people in England and 4.1% in Scotland with a learning disability go on to secure paid employment after completing their education, compared with around 80% of their peers.
Delivered in partnership with DFN Project SEARCH, Asda’s year-long Supported Internship programme combines real workplace experience with tailored education and employability training, helping young people develop the skills, confidence and experience needed to eventually move into work.
Since Asda began working with DFN Project SEARCH in 2023, 43% of interns have progressed into employment – be it with Asda or another business. With fewer than 6% of young people with learning disabilities in paid work nationally, supported internship programmes like Asda’s play a vital role in helping participants take their first steps into the workplace.
The expansion comes at a time when policymakers and employers are increasingly focused on tackling youth economic inactivity and creating more pathways into employment for young people who face barriers to work.
James Goodman, chief people officer for Asda, said: “We’re incredibly proud to be expanding our Supported Internship Programme and giving more young people with special educational needs the chance to gain real workplace experience.
“Supported internships have been shown to be an effective route into work and we’ve seen first-hand the difference these placements can make, helping young people to build confidence and take important steps towards paid employment. As we continue to grow the programme, we hope more young people can benefit from supported internships and the opportunities they create to build skills, gain experience and move into work.”
Kirsty Matthews, CEO of DFN Project SEARCH, said: “We are delighted to see the expansion of our successful programmes with Asda. Through such strong employer partnerships, we are showcasing the incredible impact that supported internships can have.
“We’re so grateful to work with companies like Asda because they demonstrate that when businesses make disability inclusion a priority, everyone benefits. These young people have so much to offer, and programmes like this give them the platform to showcase their talents and build meaningful careers. We look forward to continuing to work with Asda to reach our overall goal of supporting 10,000 young people into employment by 2030.”

items.body:
Tesco and Uber Eats launch Doorbell Drops delivery service with discounts on offer for Clubcard members
Starting today and running through to 20th September, Tesco and Uber Eats are launching Doorbell Drops, an exclusive selection of hosting essentials available at half-price to Clubcard members.
Customers can visit the Doorbell Drops hub page for Tesco on the Uber Eats app to shop the likes of Tesco Finest All Butter Sultana Scones, alongside strawberry jam and clotted cream, Mcvities Chocolate Digestives, Président French Brie with Jacobs crackers and Tesco Green Olives with Slow Roasted Tomatoes.
Merve Basci, Uber Eats UK General Manager, says: "Unannounced visits used to be a staple of British social and community life, but the fear of being unprepared and judged for stale biscuits is driving many to hide rather than host. Whether it’s dodging in-laws or frantically scouring the fridge for something edible to serve, our new partnership with Tesco can help people ditch the ‘doorbell dread’, so that young people especially can relax and enter their hosting era with more confidence."
Suzanne Quinn, Tesco Customer Director, says: “We’re always looking for little helps that make life easier for customers, and expanding our rapid delivery service through our Uber Eats partnership is another way we’re helping the nation get what they need, when they need it. The Doorbell Deals range has been created for those moments when plans change or guests arrive at short notice, giving customers quick access to fresh food, drink, and hosting essentials, so they can conveniently pull together a delicious spread in minutes.”
The launch follows Tesco’s recent partnership with Uber Eats, with the aim of extending rapid grocery delivery, Clubcard Prices and Clubcard points to more customers across the UK.

items.summary: Lord Wolfson has grown the company into Britain's biggest High Street clothing retailer, overtaking Marks & Spencer more than a decade ago.
items.body:
Next has gained from the 'Netflix effect' - will it deliver bumper profits again?
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
It is a quarter of a century since Lord Wolfson took over at Next.
In that time, he has grown the company into Britain's biggest High Street clothing retailer, overtaking Marks & Spencer more than a decade ago.
Next's share price has also soared since he took charge, rising from just under £10 to nearly £150, a performance on a par with US tech titan Microsoft.
Now valued at £17.5billion, the firm has a knack for beating even optimistic projections in its Financial results. Half-year figures due this week should see sales of £3.5billion and profit of £600million but the numbers could be higher.
Next, which sells its own brand as well as hundreds of others including Reiss, Laura Ashley and The White Company via its website, has gained from the 'Netflix effect' in which styles seen in the streaming service's dramas prove popular with shoppers at home and abroad.
Netflix effect: Next has defied the High Street gloom, can it deliver again?
Next's results will be unveiled against ever harsher conditions on the High Street.
Discount chain Primark last week said its sales were slowing, while John Lewis reported that its losses had doubled, blaming Government policies such as higher employer national insurance contributions.
Wolfson blames these rises for a 'dramatic fall' in entry level opportunities for younger people. He has also warned of the threat from Labour's Employment Rights Act calling it a 'wrecking ball' for jobs.
Next claimed a 'landmark victory' last week in its appeal against a 2024 court ruling compelling.' The firm to pay mostly female shopfloor staff the same as mostly male warehouse workers.
At the results, Wolfson is also likely to be quizzed about why Next bowed out of the race for Harvey Nichols, allowing retail entrepreneur Mike Ashley of Frasers Group to acquire the luxury Knightsbridge store.
Maybe Wolfson has his eye on another target amid the rubble of retail.

items.title: Retail foot traffic doesn’t equal sales
items.summary: Foot traffic shows where shoppers go. Transaction data reveals what happens next.
items.body:
Retail foot traffic shows which stores are attracting shoppers and where visits are increasing.
But showing up is not the same as spending.
A recent Placer.ai report named Costco and Dollar General among physical retail’s traffic leaders while describing Walmart’s visits as essentially flat. Facteus transaction data through June 2026 tells a very different story.
Foot traffic measures opportunity. Transaction data measures outcome.
Traffic cannot tell you whether a visit ended in a $130 basket, a single-item purchase, or no purchase at all. It cannot reveal whether conversion is improving, baskets are shrinking, or wallet share is shifting between competitors.
When the same four retailers are compared using observed card spend, the leaderboard nearly flips.
Data note: Spend, transaction, and average order value figures come from Facteus first-party transaction data covering June 2023 through June 2026. Visitation figures come from Placer.ai’s report, Physical Retail in 2026: How the Giants Are Winning, and are not Facteus data.
Costco is Winning Trips, but Losing Basket Momentum
Costco is the traffic report’s standout, with visits per store up 18.1% from pre-pandemic levels.
The wallet tells a more nuanced story.
Costco’s observed spend growth has slowed in every quarter since mid-2024, falling from 14.2% in Q3 2024 to 0.9% in Q1 2026 before turning negative in Q2 at -1.5%. Transactions still grew 1.5% in Q2, but average order value fell 3.0%.
Members are still coming. They are simply putting less in the basket.
A generational shift may help explain why. In H1 2026, observed Costco spend from Gen Z grew 32%, while spend from Baby Boomers fell 4.0% and Gen X declined 3.8%. Costco is attracting younger shoppers, but those shoppers currently spend less per trip than the customers pulling back.
The traffic signal is strong. The spend momentum is not.
Walmart’s Flat Traffic Hid the Strongest Wallet
Placer.ai described Walmart’s visits as essentially flat in 2025, followed by a 3.5% increase in Q1 2026.
Facteus data shows what that traffic view missed. Observed Walmart spend grew 8.6% in 2025 and accelerated to 14.2% growth in Q1 2026. When you put the Q1 figures side-by-side:
Visits grew 3.5%. Observed spend grew 14.2%.
Transactions increased 9.2%, while average order value grew 4.6%, two outcomes a traffic counter cannot measure. The strength was broad-based. In H1 2026, Walmart spend increased in every region and across every generation.
Walmart may have had the quietest traffic story. But it had the strongest wallet story.
Target’s Traffic Recovery is Real, but the Basket is the Test
Target is where traffic and transaction data most clearly agree.
Visits grew 5.1% in Q1 2026, Target’s first increase in more than a year. Facteus data confirmed the recovery at the register: transactions increased 6.4%, and observed spend grew 7.7%.
It was Target’s first positive quarter after five consecutive declines. But Q2 revealed an important caveat: transactions grew 6.8%, while average order value fell 2.2%, moderating spend growth to 4.5%.
Shoppers have returned. Their baskets have not fully recovered.
That distinction will help determine whether Target’s turnaround is durable or still dependent on promotions and trip-driving activity. For the rest of 2026, the most important number may not be Target’s visit count. It may be the basket.
Dollar General is Growing Through the Basket
Dollar General’s traffic story centers on frequency and proximity. Nearly one-quarter of visitors now shop there four or more times per month.
But in 2025, higher visit frequency did not translate into comparable wallet growth. Observed spend increased just 2.5%, while transactions declined 0.7%. But the 2026 story is stronger:
In H1 2026, Dollar General spend grew 5.7%. Transactions increased 2.2%, while average order value rose 3.4%. Average ticket increased from $21.23 in 2024 to $22.32 in the first half of 2026.
Dollar General’s current growth engine isn’t simply the additional trip. It’s the additional item.
The data also reveals an emerging geographic opportunity. Dollar General’s observed spend grew 16.8% in the West, its fastest-growing but smallest region. The retailer known for Southern convenience may be building its next growth frontier farther west.
Why Foot Traffic and Transaction Data Tell Different Stories
Foot traffic data is not wrong. But it is incomplete when viewed on its own.
Across just four retailers, the first half of 2026 produced three distinct divergences:
- Costco gained visits while its wallet momentum plateaued
- Walmart generated double-digit spend growth on the back of a quiet traffic story
- Target’s trips returned before its baskets fully recovered
CPG brands using visit share to size retail channels could overlook the retailer capturing the most incremental spend. Commercial real estate teams evaluating anchors on visitation alone could miss major differences in economic performance. And retailers benchmarking competitors solely on visits cannot distinguish between a rival gaining attention and one gaining wallet share.
Traffic tells you where consumers went. Transaction data tells you what happened next.
How Facteus Sees It
Retail teams do not need more disconnected signals. They need answers that show what changed, why it matters, and where to act. Facteus measures what happens after a shopper walks through the door using actual card transactions from more than 200 million Americans. Our data provides account-level visibility across competitors, regions, generations, and dayparts, with near-real-time insight into changing consumer behavior.
Foot traffic shows which retailers are attracting attention. Transaction data reveals which retailers are converting that attention into economic value.
The strongest view of physical retail comes from putting both signals side by side and following the dollars.
Methodology: Spend, transaction, and average order value figures reflect Facteus observed consumer card spend at Walmart, Target, Costco Wholesale, and Dollar General from June 1, 2023, through June 30, 2026. Year-over-year comparisons use matched calendar periods. Figures represent observed panel spend, not company-reported revenue. Visitation statistics are sourced from Placer.ai’s report, Physical Retail in 2026: How the Giants Are Winning.

items.title: Mike Ashley’s Frasers ousts Hugo Boss chairman
items.summary: Frasers Group, the retail empire run by Mike Ashley, has overthrown the chairman of Hugo Boss as it seeks control of the German fashion house.  The UK fashion group, which owns Sports Direct, Jack Wills and Flannels, told investors on Monday that Stephan Sturm, chairman of Hugo Boss’ supervisory board, has agreed to step aside.  [...]
items.body:
Mike Ashley’s Frasers ousts Hugo Boss chairman
Frasers Group, the retail empire run by Mike Ashley, has overthrown the chairman of Hugo Boss as it seeks control of the German fashion house.
The UK fashion group, which owns Sports Direct, Jack Wills and Flannels, told investors on Monday that Stephan Sturm, chairman of Hugo Boss’ supervisory board, has agreed to step aside.
Ashley’s firm said it has agreed with the German fashion brand that now is an “appropriate point in time for an orderly transition” of power.
“Frasers and Mr Sturm have therefore mutually agreed that Mr Sturm will step down from his position as Chairman and member of the Supervisory Board as soon as possible as permitted by Hugo Boss’ constitution,” the group said.
Frasers Group owns nearly 48 per cent of Hugo Boss and has said it wants to push this holding above 50 per cent.
In June, the company offered £1.7bn for the shares in Hugo Boss it did not already own, but this was slapped down as “inadequate” by the board of the German firm.
Frasers then appealed to shareholders in Hugo Boss, picking up about 17 per cent of the company through its €38-per-share offer, taking the value of its stake to nearly €1.5bn (£1.27bn).
The group said it will nominate Robert Palmer, a former Frasers company secretary, to Hugo Boss’s supervisory board. Frasers chief executive Michael Murray, Ashley’s son-in-law, already holds a seat on the board.
Ashley eyes control of Hugo Boss
Sturm was appointed as chairman of Hugo Boss’s supervisory board in May last year and his tenure was supposed to run until the end of the decade.
As part of the two-tier system common in German companies, Hugo Boss’s supervisory board sits above its managing board, scrutinising its work and appointing its members.
Sturm has held board roles at healthcare firm Fresnius, airline Lufthansa and the Heinz Herman Thiele foundation, which is the controlling shareholder of manufacturing giant Knorr-Bremse.
He said on Monday morning: “Following the recent changes in the Company’s shareholder structure, I believe that this is the right time for an orderly transition in the chairmanship.”
“Frasers would like to thank Mr Sturm for the contribution he has made to Hugo Boss as Chairman of the Supervisory Board and intends to work with him in the future,” Ashley’s group said.
Sturm will formally step down as chairman on October 15 and Hugo Boss said it will begin the search for his successor with immediate effect.
The London-listed firm’s push for control of the German fashion house is part of Mike Ashley’s campaign to expand into high-end fashion.
Sports Direct, which Ashley founded in 1982, surged to prominence for selling sportswear at rock-bottom prices.
But last month, Frasers snapped up struggling department store chain Harvey Nichols in a bid to boost the visibility of its luxury label, Flannels.
Frasers has garnered a reputation for taking stakes in rival companies and using these positions to make aggressive plays for change within the firm.
In 2024, Frasers built up stakes in luxury bagmaker Mulberry and online retailer Boohoo, but failed in its attempts to gain seats on the boards of both companies.
Earlier this year, Ashley launched a £166m takeover bid for Australian shoe company Accent and called for the removal of its chairman over his alleged “poor performance”.

items.title: RUTH SUNDERLAND: Why John Lewis's troubles should worry Middle Britain
items.summary: The John Lewis department store chain is a barometer for middle-aged, middle-class Britain.
items.body:
RUTH SUNDERLAND: Why John Lewis's troubles should worry Middle Britain
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
The John Lewis department store chain is a barometer for middle-aged, middle-class Britain. It embodies every obsession and unstated cultural value of the tribe: not swish, not avant-garde, not fashionable and not bothered at being scorned by Boris Johnson’s wife Carrie.
When the retailer makes a loss, as it announced a couple of days ago, something shudders deep within the bourgeois soul.
The red ink is partly down to a conscious choice to invest for the long term, and partly down to Labour having made it much more costly to employ people. But there is no getting away from the fact shoppers are more reluctant to spend on big-ticket purchases such as a new sofa.
Considering habitués of John Lewis used to be well insulated against most economic malaise, this is disquieting in a wider sense than just for the store group itself.
Many professional mid-lifers are facing a confluence of financial pressures.
Someone aged 40 to 60 is quite likely to be exposed to a mortgage, increases in food and energy bills and higher transport costs on top of school and university fees.
Frozen income tax thresholds mean their spending power is being eaten alive by fiscal drag.
Now that traditional defined benefit pensions have largely disappeared from the private sector, they need to save large amounts for retirement, via stock market-linked schemes that can go down as well as up.
Undersold: John Lewis's troubles reveal the financial pressure facing Middle Britain
Add to that the threat of redundancy and the solidity once associated with being middle-aged and middle class looks a lot wobblier.
This is not to suggest middle Britain has been driven to the brink of poverty, but that its financial position may be more fragile than its income or apparent affluence suggest.
Compared with their own parents, today’s mid-lifers are more likely to have mortgages that are larger for longer. According to the Bank of England, nearly 750,000 households on rates below 3 per cent will come off those fixes in 2026, sending payments up by an average of just over £2,000 a year.
Fiscal drag, which will last until 2030–31 at least, could have been custom-designed to hurt the middle classes. The higher-rate threshold, at which people begin to pay 40 per cent, has been frozen since 2022: by 2030–31, nearly a quarter of all taxpayers will be on this rate or the additional 45 per cent tier.
Articles on social media featuring people saying they earn healthy salaries and still feel broke attract loud mockery, but an income of £50,000 or even £100,000 is not what it was.
The Joseph Rowntree Foundation pegs its Minimum Income Standard for a couple with two young children at £77,400 in gross household earnings in its most recent calculations.
This is the level needed to achieve what members of the public regard as a socially acceptable way of life, and it includes modest holidays, socialising and occasional presents.
Not a measure of poverty, then, but perhaps it isn’t surprising people on reasonably prosperous-sounding incomes still feel hard-up.
Throw the threat, or the reality, of redundancy into the mix and it is a cocktail of precarity.
Over-50s face more of a struggle to get back into work if they lose their job and, if they do they earn 17 per cent less on average than they did before, according to Resolution Foundation research.
A generation ago, the core John Lewis customer would have been the epitome of the comfortably-off. They are still not poor, but many are much less secure.

items.summary: Iconic British brands will be showcasing their designs at London Fashion Week from Thursday against a difficult background for the luxury good sector and challenges in the high street.
items.body:
British heritage to strut its stuff on the catwalk at London Fashion Week
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
Iconic British brands will be showcasing their designs at London Fashion Week from Thursday against a difficult background for the luxury good sector and challenges in the high street.
Upmarket brands including Barbour, Burberry, McQueen and Mulberry will be among those unveiling collections. These four will be emphasising their mix of British heritage and contemporary cool.
But high street stalwart Marks & Spencer, which moved into clothing 100 years ago and now tops the YouGov style credential polls, will also be staging its first ever London Fashion womenswear and menswear show at noon on Friday at the Design Museum in Kensington.
British model Alexa Chung has designed clothes for Barbour
Those attending the event will be able to purchase everything from 12.30pm through the website or in major stores. A video will be streamed online at 6.30pm, giving everyone else the chance to do so. The deployment of this ‘see-now, buy-now’ format, pioneered by Burberry in 2016, underlines M&S’s confidence that it has definitely ditched its frumpy reputation.
On Thursday Barbour, the 132-year old family-owned company famed for its waxed jackets with tartan linings which sell in 55 countries and are worn by the Princess of Wales, will showcase its collection at the Saatchi Gallery. Barbour’s Bedale and Beaufort jackets are still made in its factory in South Shields.
On Saturday, McQueen show will be under scrutiny by fashionistas and luxury goods analysts. This couture house, founded by the late Alexander McQueen, dresses the Princess of Wales for formal occasions.
But its interest to the City lies in its ownership. McQueen is a division of the French luxury giant Kering whose empire also includes Gucci. Kering shares are down by 21 per cent this year and by 65 per cent over the past five years. The luxury goods industry has been hard hit by the Chinese consumer slowdown, higher costs and geopolitical tensions.
Shares in Mulberry, the Somerset-based luxury handbag company, are moving upwards, however, jumping by 165 per cent since January. This is thanks to a return to sales growth driven by an emphasis its artisan roots.
When the company displays its lines on Saturday, some will be watching whether Mike Ashley, founder of Frasers, will be in the audience.
Frasers has a 37 per cent stake in Mulberry. His 2024 takeover bid for the business failed. But Ashley is eager to expand his luxury ‘eco-system’ to which he recently added the Knightsbridge store Harvey Nichols.
Burberry, the outerwear group founded in 1856, closes London Fashion Week on Monday September 21. The 19 per cent fall in the shares this year means that it must demonstrate its appeal to younger aspirational shoppers.
Burberry, a brand still in turnaround, has been successfully winning back this clientele. But sentiment remains depressed. Analysts will be looking for pieces that appeal to Americans of all ages. items.body:
Here’s why late online shopping and delivery move is a gamble worth taking for value retailer Primark
Last week there was back slapping aplenty among online guru industry observers, accompanied by an onslaught of smug, self-congratulatory 'I told you so' LinkedIn posts, as Primark announced plans to finally launch a home delivery service in Britain.
This follows the purchase of an automated fulfilment facility in Sheffield. The retailer went live with a Click and Collect service in 2022, and owner Associated British Foods (ABF) now says there is "opportunity for profitable growth" through home deliveries.
The move, which was denied following media reports earlier this year, comes as Primark prepares to split from ABF. This is likely to complete in December 2027 and is expected to create two new FTSE 100 companies, with analysts predicting that Primark could be valued at as much as £9 billion, and the food part of the business £4 billion.
A spokesperson commented: “Our stores will always be at the heart of Primark. But a lot has changed in online retail in recent years, from how customers shop and their expectations for online delivery. Combined with the digital progress we’ve made, and particularly the success of Click & Collect, we’re confident the time is right to give customers in Great Britain even more choice in how they shop with us.”
Sorry, online gurus, but Primark launching home delivery doesn’t mean it was wrong to resist the rise and rise of e-commerce. In fact, it might actually have been pursuing the right strategy all along. For years, Primark trod its own path: significant store footfall and no home delivery in the face of everyone else rushing online. But, as the Primark spokesperson says, things change.
Conventional wisdom dictates that, if a retailer can sell online, it should. But for Primark, the numbers didn't stack up, and it has said as much on numerous occasions over the past few years. Low prices versus picking and packing, delivery, and the never ending headache that is customer returns. No thanks!
So, ultimately, this isn't about Primark being a laggard that is finally catching up. It has spent years building a mighty store led model. And it has acted in a thoughtful, measured manner. It tested the waters by introducing Click and Collect, and now it is stumping up serious amounts of cash for the infrastructure needed to make home delivery work at scale.
The argument in favour of this move is a compelling one. I'm a fan of Primark but I rarely shop there in person these days thanks to the busy aisles and massive queues (although the latter has been addressed to a certain extent with the roll-out of self-service checkouts). This is about making Primark accessible to people like me who currently avoid the physical store experience altogether. Open up a completely new customer segment and you’ve bagged yourself the Holy Grail of omnichannel retail.
Nonetheless, the question remains, is it possible to make the economics around online shopping and delivery work at Primark prices? That's another article in itself. Let us know your thoughts in the comments section below.

items.body:
Ocado Retail reports online grocery delivery milestone as company hits 600,000 orders in one week
Ocado Retail, part of grocery technology and retail specialist Ocado Group and the operator of Ocado.com, a joint venture with Marks and Spencer, has racked up 600,000 orders in a single week.
In a LinkedIn post, the venture said: "What a week! Reaching a milestone of this scale takes incredible dedication, teamwork, and effort from every single person across our business. To mark the achievement, we brought the celebration into the office with plenty of team spirit, decorations, sweet treats, and a competition giving colleagues the chance to win even more Ocado goodies!"
Reaching over 80% of the UK population, Ocado lays claim to more than one million active customers and a range of around 50,000 products (including big name brands, over 7,000 items from the M&S food and drink range and Ocado’s Own-Range).
To put the 600,000 milestone in context, UK market leader Tesco currently handles over 1.2 million online grocery orders each week.
South Korea
Ocado Group recently launched its first customer fulfilment centre (CFC) with Lotte Shopping in South Korea. Following a partnership deal inked in 2022, last year Lotte went live with the Ocado Smart Platform, fulfilling orders using Ocado's in-store fulfilment (ISF) software. And now the first automated CFC will serve a catchment covering four million households across Busan and the broader Yeongnam region.
It also introduces a number of innovations for the first time. These include the launch of Ocado's fully automated freezer (Auto-Freezer), bringing Ocado's proprietary 'hive and bot' automation into temperatures as low as -25° C. The site will also support dawn delivery, enabling freshly packed grocery orders to reach customers’ homes before 7am.
It is also expected to be the most environmentally efficient Ocado CFC in the world, supporting a 100% electric vehicle fleet for daytime deliveries and operating more energy efficient 3D printed bots, with multi-temperature totes to maximise storage density for delivery. The widespread installation of solar panels will reduce annual carbon emissions by over 1,000 tonnes, those involved claim.
Nick De La Vega, Chief Revenue Officer, Ocado Group, said: “This is another major milestone for Ocado as we launch one of our most advanced CFCs to date in one of the world's leading markets for grocery e-commerce. Online is fast becoming the main grocery channel for many customers across South Korea, and we are excited to help Lotte deliver a step-change in the choice, service and experience it offers shoppers."
Cha Woo Chul, Chief Executive Officer, Lotte Mart & Super, said: “ZETTA Smartcentre Busan is a next-generation online logistics centre combining Lotte Mart’s fresh food expertise with UK Ocado’s AI robot logistics technology. By delivering farm-fresh produce on schedule to four million households in the Yeongnam region, we will reshape the paradigm of domestic online grocery shopping. Backed by world class robot automation technology, eco-friendly management, safety control, and the creation of 2,000 local jobs, we will establish a model of a trusted, sustainable future logistics centre for customers in the Yeongnam region.”

He added: “A huge thank you to our presenters for your time, energy and expertise, and to our teams for high engagement levels throughout the day (pizza helped). Days like this matter - they keep us curious, connected and ready for what's next.”
So hot right now
Fynd is included in RTIH’s first ever Retail Technology Hot 100 List. Launching in August, this sees us bringing you the hottest companies whose solutions and systems are helping drive the retail sector forward.
Our Founder and Editor, Scott Thompson, drew up a list of 150 companies that had consistently been on his radar over the past 12 months whilst bringing our community the latest retail tech news and views that matter. These companies operate across the omnichannel retail landscape (stores, online, mobile, supply chain, payments etc).
Our judging panel, including Vineta Bajaj, Group CFO, Holland & Barrett, Dan McGrath, JD Group Customer Operations, JD Sports, Dr. Astha Purohit, Director of Product Management, Customer Data and Identity, Walmart, and Paula Bobbett, Chief Data and Digital Officer, Boots, provided feedback on those who have the most innovative, forward thinking technology offerings and are also best addressing retailers' current challenges, painpoints, and opportunities.
The judges used the following framework when making their picks:
1. Retailer problem fit - how meaningful, strategic, and widely felt the retailer pain being addressed is.
2. Production traction in retail (2025–2026) - real named retailer deployments, pilots. 
3. Innovation and defensibility - genuine technical novelty paired with a defensible competitive position.
And there was also a public vote, with thousands of members of our community of retail tech enthusiasts getting involved. Thanks to all those who took part! Based on the judging panel's feedback and the public vote, we then drew up our first ever RTIH Retail Technology Hot 100.
So, without further ado, here are the 100 hottest global retail technology ventures right now. Drum roll, please…

items.body:
UK consumer sentiment rises but feel good factor could fade away as Golden Quarter approaches
PwC research shows improving household finances and lower inflation expectations sparking a UK consumer confidence rebound at a five-year high. Its survey recorded an index score of +1 in August, after a sharp fall in April to –13 as fears over the cost-of-living gripped consumers as conflict continued in the Middle East.
Now, after the hottest UK summer on record, the index score has reversed that decline and is now two points higher than in January, continuing the upward trend since the start of last year. Sentiment saw an increase across all age groups, with 35 to 44-year-olds in particular seeing their sentiment reach its highest ever recorded level of +21. Sentiment among over 65s also rebounded to its highest level since the removal of winter fuel allowance was announced in autumn 2024, overtaking both the 54 to 65 and 45 to 54 age groups.
The findings show perceived household finances are at the strongest they have been in the last four years, improving across every demographic. 39% of those surveyed describing their financial situation as 'healthy' - i.e. that they have money left over at the end of the month for luxuries or savings - up from 27% in September 2022. At the other end of the spectrum, among the least affluent ‘E2’ socioeconomic group, the proportion of those either struggling to pay bills or having missed bill payments altogether has fallen from 28% to 12% over the same period.
This combined with a period of real earnings growth, falling food inflation, and lower consumer inflation expectations have contributed to consumers feeling more buoyant. The findings also show that fewer consumers plan to make short-term spending cutbacks than in the spring. 68% plan to make some kind of spending cutback in the next three months, compared with 78% in April.
However, the growth in confidence is still tempered by worries about the cost of living, with 85% of consumers citing this as one of their top concerns alongside the UK economy (86%). While both figures are down from April, they are roughly at the same level as they were at start of the year. Consumers’ levels of concern are largely unchanged from January, with the environment and global warming being the only issue to become more pressing - 75% of consumers cite this as a concern, up from 71% at the start of the year, in the wake of recent heatwaves.
Concerns amongst different demographic groups show a more nuanced picture. For young people, 61% of 18 to 24 year-olds say they're worried about job prospects or job security, up from 54% in January. Amongst those aged 25 to 34, concerns around mortgage repayments or rent increases rose from 52% to 62% over the same period.
Sam Waller, Leader of Industry for Consumer Markets at PwC UK, says: "The World Cup and the heatwave have helped spur a welcome uplift in consumer sentiment. But our survey shows consumer caution hasn't gone away. Cost of living pressures remain, and for some are an increasing concern."
"As we head into autumn, the pressure on household finances will increase as energy and food prices rise. This will impact consumer facing businesses – along with wider macroeconomic headwinds that could spell higher interest rates and possible tax rises. Businesses should incentivise customers to start Christmas shopping now, and at the same, they must prepare themselves for a slowdown in consumer demand, look for ways to optimise operating costs, and to get their back of house in order."
At the time of the survey in mid-August, 14% of consumers polled said that they had already started their Christmas shopping. A further 16% said that they planned to do most of their Christmas shopping earlier than usual, even though they had not started yet, compared with only 4% saying they would make most of their festive purchases later.
Meanwhile, for the first time since the end of the pandemic, more consumers said that they expected to spend more this year on Christmas shopping and celebrations rather than less. Some 25% thought they would spend more in the run up to this Christmas - up from 22% a year ago - compared with only 21% expecting to spend less - down from 26% in September 2025.
For those intending to spend more this year, the top reason was that it is ‘important to keep Christmas special' (cited by 33%), while 32% said it was because they had saved up throughout the year. For those who plan to spend less on Christmas this year, the rising cost of living (73%) was their number one reason.
Jacqueline Windsor, Head of Retail at PwC UK, says: "For retailers, Christmas needs to come early. Consumer sentiment has hit positive territory for the first time since the pandemic, and some people have already started festive shopping. It's a golden period of consumer confidence that may have come too early for the Golden Quarter. We expect food and fuel inflation to bite in the autumn, and added uncertainty as the new Chancellor assesses if any tax changes may be needed in the upcoming budget. Retailers would do well to strike early with Christmas before purse strings tighten."
