items.title: Burnham told to deliver 10 per cent hospitality VAT after backing tax cut
items.summary: More than 800 hospitality businesses have called on Andy Burnham to make good on his support for lower VAT, piling pressure on the prime minister ahead of next month’s Budget. Pub giants, restaurant chains, hotels and some of Britain’s best-known chefs have signed an open letter demanding the government cut hospitality VAT from 20 per [...]
items.body:
Burnham told to deliver 10 per cent hospitality VAT after backing tax cut
More than 800 hospitality businesses have called on Andy Burnham to make good on his support for lower VAT, piling pressure on the prime minister ahead of next month’s Budget.
Pub giants, restaurant chains, hotels and some of Britain’s best-known chefs have signed an open letter demanding the government cut hospitality VAT from 20 per cent to 10 per cent.
Signatories include JD Wetherspoon, Greene King, Fuller’s, Pizza Express, Wagamama, Marriott and Center Parcs, alongside chefs Tom Kerridge, Heston Blumenthal, Angela Hartnett and Jason Atherton.
The intervention puts Burnham’s own words back in front of him after he said in February, while mayor of Greater Manchester, that he would “argue for a VAT rate more consistent with what you find in Europe”.
“We don’t need another promise. We need action,” Kerridge said. The campaign lands at an awkward moment for the government after Burnham acknowledged last week that the “cost of doing business is too high”, while also warning that limited public finances left him with little room for manoeuvre.
It also comes days after ministers confirmed plans to allow regional authorities to impose an uncapped levy on overnight stays, triggering a fresh backlash from hotels and tourism businesses.
Hospitality sector piles pressure on Burnham
Britain charges hospitality businesses VAT at 20 per cent, compared with 10 per cent in France, Italy and Spain and seven per cent in Germany.
More than 370,000 people have now signed the #VATsTheProblem petition calling for the UK rate to be cut to 10 per cent.
“It’s time for a fairer tax burden for hospitality,” the businesses wrote. “Without action, closures will only continue to accelerate, jobs will continue to be lost and opportunities for young people reduced.”
Kerridge argued the tax hits hospitality particularly hard because labour represents such a large share of costs.
“You can reclaim VAT on a product, but you can’t reclaim VAT on a person,” he said.
Businesses are also absorbing higher wages, energy and food bills, while the sector has lost around 100,000 jobs over the past two years.
Greene King, Hilton and Wahaca backed the campaign earlier this year, while Fuller’s chief executive Simon Emeny previously told City AM that cutting VAT to 10 per cent was “critical” to returning the industry to growth.
Burnham has already offered the sector an olive branch since entering Downing Street, announcing a 20 per cent business rates cut for pubs, clubs and live music venues during his first week in office.
He indicated last week that the government could go further at the 28 October Budget, saying ministers would look at business rates more broadly for high street firms.
But the prime minister stopped short of promising further tax cuts. “I wouldn’t want to promise the earth,” Burnham said, adding that he was facing a “difficult financial outlook”.
Hospitality bosses now want him to add the VAT pledge he made before entering Downing Street to that Budget package.
“A lower rate of VAT for hospitality can turn closures into openings, lost jobs into new jobs, and boarded up high streets into thriving centres of community,” the letter said.

items.title: The perilous economic conditions facing the UK can be traced back to Trump | Richard Partington
items.summary: As John Healey drafts his autumn budget, the US president’s policies continue to inflate debt servicing costs Britain is not entirely in control of its own destiny, from the rising cost of the weekly shop, to the vaulting cost of government borrowing. What is said and done in Westminster matters. But the global backdrop is making life tough, not least in the deeds and words of one man: Donald Trump. As John Healey drafts his plan for next month’s autumn budget, the perilous economic conditions the chancellor must navigate can be traced back to the door of the US president. Continue reading...
items.body:
Britain is not entirely in control of its own destiny, from the rising cost of the weekly shop, to the vaulting cost of government borrowing. What is said and done in Westminster matters. But the global backdrop is making life tough, not least in the deeds and words of one man: Donald Trump.
As John Healey drafts his plan for next month’s autumn budget, the perilous economic conditions the chancellor must navigate can be traced back to the door of the US president.
The US-Israel war on Iran is driving up inflation, amid the most serious shock to oil and gas prices of the modern age. The global financial market turmoil this has triggered is adding to the debt servicing costs of governments worldwide, in a situation made worse by Trump’s reckless fiscal policy and threats of interference at the US Federal Reserve.
Meanwhile, there was a grim irony last week as Healey travelled to Coventry for his first big speech as chancellor on the same day that Jaguar Land Rover – with its headquarters just down the road – announced 4,000 job cuts, as Trump’s tariff policies throttle the car industry. The president’s geopolitical posturing and steps to dismantle the post-second world war western security consensus are also adding to pressure on Healey to ramp up defence spending.
In his speech, Healey did not directly call out the source of these economic headwinds sweeping in from across the Atlantic. But he was wistful about the timing of his appointment as chancellor.
“In our British democratic system, if you have the privilege to serve, you don’t get to choose: you don’t get to choose the time, you don’t get to choose the circumstances,” he said.
There are, though, signs of resilience. Last week, the chancellor received a pre-budget boost from figures showing that Britain’s economy unexpectedly shrugged off the worst of the Middle East fallout to grow at a robust pace in July, helped by the rapid expansion of AI.
Far from sitting back and blaming the US for all of the country’s problems, the chancellor also recognises there are meaningful steps that Labour can take to cushion the blow, and to help rebuild confidence.
However, last week was still a bad one, as the latest flare-up in the Iran war drove the oil price to $109 a barrel and fuelled a dramatic bond market selloff. As an open economy in the eye of the storm, the yield – in effect the interest rate – on 10-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, rose to almost 5.4%; the highest level for almost two decades.
The renewed bout of selling pressure in the financial markets could not have happened at a worse time for Healey.
History suggests that the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) may need to use the latest gyrations in markets to form the basis of its budget forecast. With this report informing the boundaries of the chancellor’s tax and spending plans, Healey could find himself boxed in.
Back in spring, the Treasury watchdog used the market movements over the 10 working days to 30 January as the input for Rachel Reeves’s spring statement – leaving roughly a month gap before her 3 March Commons set piece. For Healey, there are just over six weeks before his budget on 28 October.
Should the reference period use current market conditions, analysts at Oxford Economics estimate the headroom against the main fiscal rule of £23.6bn – left by Reeves in March – could be halved.
In previous years, the OBR has taken a flexible approach in times of elevated market volatility, and so there is no guarantee this will be the case. There are also other variables that are hard to forecast; from growth to inflation, and from the jobs market to the level of immigration.
However, the risk is that the bond market meltdown will have a deleterious impact on the forecast, making the fiscal arithmetic for Healey significantly tougher amid myriad spending pressures for Labour to finance.
This week could also prove critical. On Tuesday, official figures are expected to show a further slowdown in Britain’s jobs market, including weaker levels of wage growth and a rise in unemployment. Inflation figures on Wednesday are predicted to show a rise in the headline rate in August to above 3%, in a renewed squeeze on living standards.
In the midst of all this, the Bank of England will take its next decision on interest rates on Thursday, in a verdict that will play a crucial role in influencing the borrowing costs of households, businesses and the government.
With a cooling domestic jobs market, and amid global turbulence over which Threadneedle Street has little control, the City predicts interest rates will be kept on hold. However, this will add to the sense that Britain is without a full grip on its future.
For the government, too, there is a growing sense that some of Andy Burnham’s biggest fiscal decisions could be deferred beyond the budget to next year’s comprehensive spending review.
Such a strategy will give him more time to get things right on knotty issues such as social care, welfare and defence spending, but it will also avoid tempting fate – Liz Truss style – with an expansive budget in the midst of a global storm.
Since the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street crash there has been a saying among economists that “when America sneezes, the rest of the world catches a cold”. Almost a century on, it is clear the White House under Trump has infected the world economy, and with it Britain.

Tillo acquires Amilon and looks to establish dominance in rewards, incentives and gift cards space
Tillo, a rewards, incentives and gift card platform, has announced the acquisition of and a partnership with Amilon, a specialist in digital incentives, gift cards, and employee benefits in Italy. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.
Collectively, Tillo and Amilon expect to process over £3 billion worth of gift cards in 2026 and grow 30% year-over-year.
“This is an incredibly exciting landmark moment for Tillo and for our industry. From our very first conversations with the Amilon team, it was clear we shared the same belief in where rewards, incentives and engagement are heading, and the role they play in creating genuine connections between brands, businesses, and consumers,” says Alex Preece, CEO and Co-Founder at Tillo.
“Amilon has built an outstanding business over two decades, trusted by leading Italian and international enterprises and known for exceptional standards of service and expertise. Joining forces gives us the opportunity to combine our strengths and build an international digital value platform with the depth and reach to shape the future of this industry. Equally important, we've found a team whose culture and values strongly align with our own, and I'm proud to welcome them as partners into the Tillo Group.”
The clock is ticking: there are now just three weeks left to get your entries in for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
The eighth edition of the RTIH Innovation Awards is now up and running with the deadline for entries being Friday, 2nd October. That’s just three weeks away, so don’t delay, start working on your submissions today!
The awards, sponsored by 3D Cloud, Business France, and Retail Technology Show 2027, celebrate global tech innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world. Our latest winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC (Prince Consort Rooms) in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
Click here for FAQs, categories, and information on our judging panel.
Sign up for an account and submit your entry or entries here.
Mastercard unveils Payeux Tapestry in London and agentic AI research predicting £370 billion spend by 2030
One in ten consumers will routinely use artificial intelligence to shop and pay by 2030, according to a report published by Mastercard that surveyed 26,000 people across Europe and canvassed the opinions of four futurologists. The report was unveiled in London this week and forecasts AI driven consumer spending will hit £370 billion a year globally by the end of the decade.
Carried out in June and July this year in conjunction with Opinium who questioned 13,000 teens and 13,00 parents in pairs across 13 European nations from France and Germany to Italy, Spain, and the UK, the research showed 18% of teens already use an AI assistant, such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, once a week to help them compare products before purchasing. This compares to 9% for the parental adults surveyed.
A third of the surveyed teens said they would happily hand over control to a fully AI run shopping assistant that chooses and pays for products. Speaking at a press event to launch the research, Agnes Woolrich, SVP MasterCard UK, commented: "AI has transformational potential."
"Businesses will have to think differently," she argued, in an exclusive chat with RTIH, who were in attendance at the event prior to the research’s wider general release on 8th September. Woolrich added: "Investments in retailers’ brand, loyalty programmes, and in machine readable digital estates will all be essential in the future, as agentic AI adoption advances."
“I expect the technology to follow the classic adoption curve with early adopters right through to laggards evident. This goes for consumers and merchants," she said, while also unveiling a new artwork commissioned to accompany the report that apes the famous Bayreux Tapestry.
Morrisons teams with Instacart owned Instaleap to boost online marketplace and in-store fulfilment
Instaleap, a company providing software for e‑commerce fulfillment and last mile operations that was recently bought by Instacart, and Morrisons have announced a new partnership.
“We’re proud to partner with Morrisons, one of the UK’s most respected grocery retailers, as they continue to strengthen their omnichannel offering,” says Antonio Nunes, Head of Instaleap. "Consumers now increasingly expect ordering from their local supermarket to be as easy as ordering take-away. Meeting that demand at scale - efficiently, reliably - takes technology built specifically for grocery. That's exactly what we're giving Morrisons."
“We’re constantly looking for ways to make online grocery shopping easier and more convenient,” says Charlotte Exell, Group Online Director at Morrisons. “More of our customers are choosing to shop from us through one of our immediacy partners and they expect an efficient, dependable service every time. Working with Instaleap powers our online operations behind the scenes, helping us deliver fresh groceries directly to our customers’ doors quickly and reliably.”
Everseen, Hanshow and OpenAI top first ever RTIH Retail Technology Hot 100 List
In partnership with 3D Cloud, RTIH is pleased to launch its first ever Retail Technology Hot 100 List. We’re bringing you the hottest companies whose solutions and systems are helping drive the retail sector forward.
Our Founder and Editor, Scott Thompson, drew up a list of 150 companies that had consistently been on his radar over the past 12 months whilst bringing our community the latest retail tech news and views that matter. These companies operate across the omnichannel retail landscape (stores, online, mobile, supply chain, payments etc).
Our judging panel, including Vineta Bajaj, Group CFO, Holland & Barrett, Dan McGrath, JD Group Customer Operations, JD Sports, Dr. Astha Purohit, Director of Product Management, Customer Data and Identity, Walmart, and Paula Bobbett, Chief Data and Digital Officer, Boots, provided feedback on those who have the most innovative, forward thinking technology offerings and are also best addressing retailers' current challenges, painpoints, and opportunities.
The judges used the following framework when making their picks:
1. Retailer problem fit - how meaningful, strategic, and widely felt the retailer pain being addressed is.
2. Production traction in retail (2025–2026) - real named retailer deployments, pilots. 
3. Innovation and defensibility - genuine technical novelty paired with a defensible competitive position.
And there was also a public vote, with thousands of members of our community of retail tech enthusiasts getting involved. Thanks to all those who took part! Based on the judging panel's feedback and the public vote, we then drew up our first ever RTIH Retail Technology Hot 100.
So, without further ado, here are the 100 hottest global retail technology ventures right now. Drum roll, please…
Cinema chain Vue unveils new look Finchley Road, London venue including arrival of Vue Your Way
Vue has unveiled its transformed Vue Finchley Road location in London as the company invests in enhancing the big screen experience for customers. The refurbished venue features Lux and Ultra Lux seating, Laser by Barco projection technology, an expanded hot food offering and the arrival of Vue Your Way, making Finchley Road the first London venue to introduce this concept.
With Vue Your Way, people can download their tickets to their wallets to speed up the entrance process. They can scan their QR code at the ticket gates and head on through to build their own snack combos. They then pay at self-service checkouts, with staff members on hand if any issues occur, before heading into their screen to, hopefully, lose themselves in a good movie.
A spokesperson for Vue said: “This latest investment reflects our ongoing commitment to delivering the very best in big screen entertainment, combining industry leading technology with more personalised and flexible experiences for our customers. Thank you to our colleagues, partners and local community for supporting us throughout the refurbishment. We look forward to welcoming guests to experience the next chapter of Vue Finchley Road.”
Hotel Chocolat agrees exclusive tie up that brings retailer on to Deliveroo quick commerce platform
Hotel Chocolat has announced an exclusive partnership with Deliveroo, launching initially with five of its locations - Manchester Cross Street, Chiswick, Staines, St James's and Wimbledon. Customers will be able to shop the Velvetiser, Hotel Chocolat's new boxed selections, its signature selectors, and Velvetised Creams.
Carrie Martin, UK General Manager at Hotel Chocolat, says: “Thoughtful gifting has always been at the heart of what we do, and we're constantly looking at how we can make it easier for customers to mark the moments that matter.”
“Partnering with Deliveroo gives customers a completely new way to access and send Hotel Chocolat gifts: combining the quality and originality they expect from us with greater choice and flexibility. It’s an exciting next step in how we’re growing the brand and meeting customers where they want to shop.”
Suzy McClintock, VP Consumer at Deliveroo, says: “We are building a new destination for gifting at Deliveroo. Customers are no longer using our platform just to shop for themselves but to send something special to a loved one, whether for Valentine’s Day, Christmas, a birthday and more. As a true gifting specialist, Hotel Chocolat brings real brand authority and category expertise to our retail offer, and we are excited to help them reach more consumers who are on a mission to find a meaningful last minute gift.”
Paul Stafford goes from client to colleague as he swaps The Very Group for new role at EPAM Systems
Paul Stafford has joined Empathy Lab, an Al native agency launched by EPAM Systems, as Senior Director - Retail Media EMEA. He was previously at The Very Group and has also worked at Superdrug and PepsiCo.
Stafford played an integral role in launching Superdrug’s retail media network Optimo, before joining The Very Group last year to lead its retail media proposition.
In a LinkedIn post, he said: “My retail media journey continues…Last week I joined the Empathy Lab by EPAM team at EPAM Systems as Senior Director - Retail Media Consulting, looking after EMEA. I've gone from client to colleague with one of the sharpest minds in retail nedia, Diana Abebrese, and am looking forward to learning from her and the wider team (and hopefully teaching them a thing or two.”
He added: “I couldn't be more excited to build strategies and solutions for our clients, from revenue generation and media planning through to agentic tooling and orchestration. In the short space of time I've been here I've genuinely been blown away by some of the projects already in flow for so many global retailers, agencies and brands.”

items.title: Tesco alerts police as supermarket becomes latest victim of scam ‘endorsement’ ads
items.summary: Exclusive: Supermarket joins line of firms and sports stars including Bellingham and Haaland to have their image hijacked via ads Tesco has alerted City of London police after it became the latest in a string of companies and sports stars, including Barclays bank and Lewis Hamilton, to have its image hijacked in a “scam” by unlicensed casinos advertising via Facebook and Instagram. The supermarket chain is among several household-name businesses to have been targeted in an apparent effort by casinos that cannot legally operate in Britain to capitalise on their brand recognition. Continue reading...
items.body:
Tesco has alerted City of London police after it became the latest in a string of companies and sports stars, including Barclays bank and Lewis Hamilton, to have its image hijacked in a “scam” by unlicensed casinos advertising via Facebook and Instagram.
The supermarket chain is among several household-name businesses to have been targeted in an apparent effort by casinos that cannot legally operate in Britain to capitalise on their brand recognition.
Their branding has featured in ads and websites, promoted via the US social media company Meta, that gave the false impression that the businesses had launched their own casinos.
Sports stars including Lewis Hamilton and Tyson Fury have also had their faces used without consent, while one offshore casino used a lookalike of the footballer Erling Haaland wearing a Norway shirt.
England’s Jude Bellingham and the Manchester United player Bruno Fernandes have also previously had their images used without consent by rogue gambling firms.
Both the Gambling Commission and the Advertising Standards Authority are aware of the problem, but appear to have had little success in preventing the spread of the ads.
A fake “Tesco casino” was advertised on Facebook and even had its own page on the platform until the Guardian sent questions to the social media site’s owner, Meta.
The ads were linked to a website, which is still accessible in the UK, that claims to be “the official Tesco casino”.
The site boasts that its slot machine games are “laid out as clearly as the aisles at a Tesco Extra” and claims that its casino is “built on the trust of Tesco, a FTSE 100 company with 107 years of UK trading history since 1919”.
However, it does not have a licence to provide gambling services in Great Britain, a legal requirement to operate.
Tesco declined to comment but the supermarket chain referred its concerns to the National Cyber Security Centre and Report Fraud service, run by City of London police. A spokesperson for City of London police said it had received the complaint but had not yet referred it to a police force for investigation “at this time”.
Barclays’ branding has been co-opted in promotional material that features the face of Lewis Hamilton.
In one Facebook advert for “Barclays Slots”, now taken down, an apparently AI-generated woman had her trousers pulled down to expose her buttocks. She then turned round to reveal that she was playing a Barclays casino game on her phone.
Barclays said it “does not endorse or have any involvement” with the material, and took appropriate action to protect customers from misleading use of its intellectual property.
Other ads that featured on Facebook and Instagram promoted fake casinos including Monzo slots, using the online bank’s imagery.
Monzo said this was an “AI-enabled scam where criminals take advantage of our much-loved brand to trick people”, and urged its customers to be alert to such material.
Meta said it had taken down the ads after the Guardian’s inquiries. But the company is understood to believe that advertisers – not its platforms – are responsible for complying with local regulations.
The boxer Tyson Fury responded to the appearance of an online casino bearing his name by filming a video for his Instagram followers, disavowing any involvement.
He said he had turned down “millions” offered by gambling companies in the past, and would never promote the industry. There is no suggestion the fake Tyson Fury casino was advertised on Meta platforms.
One cryptocurrency casino called Rainbet, which claims to be licensed by the Indian ocean island of Anjouan, uses an apparent lookalike of Manchester City and Norway striker Erling Haaland acting as a casino croupier, wearing a Norway top.
The site is not available to users in the UK, but was advertised via Meta.
Legitimate gambling companies, including Coral and Gala Bingo, have also fallen victim to the apparent deliberate impersonation by unlicensed casinos.
Bejay Patel, the managing director of UK and Ireland at Entain, which owns both brands, said any casino masquerading as a licensed operator was “exploiting British consumers and legitimate businesses alike and paying no taxes, while some of the world’s largest technology platforms continue to profit from hosting their adverts”.
He added: “Ofcom needs to take a harder line on the companies facilitating this activity.”
The Gambling Commission has previously criticised Meta’s failure to act on unlicensed casinos, as the regulator struggles to keep a lid on a surge in rogue casinos.
The commission said: “Illegal activity linked to gambling is a threat we take seriously, and using a trusted brand’s identity to funnel people towards unlicensed casino products is a particularly cynical version of it.”
It said it would act to take down unlicensed websites that target UK consumers and would be better able to do so from autumn, when it will get more powers as a result of the crime and policing bill.
The unauthorised use of intellectual property is outside the commission’s remit. The regulator said it was working with the ASA.
Several of the sites analysed by the Guardian claim to be licensed in Curacao, a Caribbean former Dutch colony that is known as a haven for online gambling companies that do not have a licence in big economies such as the UK or US.
That means that any which offer their services to British customers are doing so illegally.
The Tyson Fury-branded casino and Tesco casino appear to be targeting UK consumers, but link to a contact page did not work. In the case of the Tyson Fury casino, it led to a page that simply contained the text: “Silence is golden.”
The Guardian has approached representatives of Haaland and Hamilton for comment.

items.title: Iceland to open first store in the Falklands
items.summary: Boss Lord Richard Walker says it would be the the first UK high street brand to operate there.
items.body:
Iceland to open first store in the Falklands
- Published
Supermarket Iceland is opening its first branch in the Falkland Islands, according to boss Lord Richard Walker.
He said the store would be opening in December, adding on LinkedIn it would be the the first UK high street brand to open there.
The shop will be in the capital Stanley where it will serve a population of about 3,500.
Lord Walker said the Welsh business, based in Deeside, in Flintshire, was growing internationally and he wanted to expand it further.
"We actually wholesale or franchise to over 75 different countries," he said.
"And we've had our eye on the Falkland Islands for quite a long time. We think it's a very underserved market, with a lack of competition, and, of course, being that our product is predominantly frozen, it transports and exports very well."
The said the timing was coincidental "given the geopolitics", Lord Walker told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast.
Argentine president Javier Milei recently claimed the islands - referred to as Las Malvinas by Argentina - were "historically and legally" Argentinian.
The Stanley store would be in partnership with Kelper Stores, part of the Fortuna group.
Lord Walker said he would be visting the island to cut the ribbon and open the supermarket.
"We estimate that prices will be almost 30% lower than other competitors on the island," he said.
"And I think that's really going to bring some much needed value to the market."

items.title: 'Skimpflation' warning as tinned mackerel alternative hits more supermarket shelves
items.summary: Consumer group Which? has called the sale of jack mackerel, a cheaper, less nutritious species of fish, an example of "skimpflation".
items.body:
'Skimpflation' warning as tinned mackerel alternative hits more supermarket shelves
- Published
A growing trend of supermarkets selling a cheaper, less nutritious alternative to tinned mackerel is an example of "skimpflation", a consumer group has said.
Princes - which supplies major supermarkets - has substituted jack mackerel, an entirely different species, for mackerel, with similar tins also being sold by Lidl.
The switch has been spurred by dwindling stocks of Atlantic mackerel after years of overfishing, with its Chilean counterpart more sustainable and a third of the cost.
"It's a real concern when manufacturers quietly downgrade everyday staples like these as shoppers can end up paying the same price for a product that delivers significantly less nutritional quality," Sue Davies, head of food policy at Which?, said.
Jack mackerel contains about half as much omega-3 and around a third as much vitamin B12 as traditional mackerel.
The shift has prompted complaints from some consumers over differences in taste and texture, as well as concerns about how clearly the replacement fish is being labelled.
Princes announced last October, external that it was changing all of its tinned mackerel products to jack mackerel, saying the species meets the Marine Stewardship Council's sustainability standards.
The firm said its jack mackerel products were "clearly identified" and had been introduced following extensive product and consumer testing, describing it as having a "milder flavour and meatier texture".
Lidl is selling jack mackerel under its house brand. Lidl GB said it was "committed to sourcing fish and seafood from responsibly managed fisheries".
Davies from Which? said: "While manufacturers face genuine supply chain pressures and sustainability challenges, they have a responsibility to shoppers to be completely upfront when they change a product's recipe."
She added: "Skimpflation - quietly changing ingredients to cut costs - has become increasingly common, but it can feel particularly sneaky as shoppers may not realise a product has changed until they get it home and eat it."
'Mackerel war'
Despite its name, jack mackerel is not a type of mackerel. Jack mackerel belongs to the Carangidae fish family, while traditional mackerel belongs to the Scombridae family.
Until December 2025, under UK law, Carangidae species could only be marketed as "jack", "scad", "trevally" or "horse mackerel".
But shortly after Princes launched its new product as "jack mackerel", the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs changed its rules to permit the labelling.
Industry figures reposted by seafood market intelligence platform Undercurrent suggest wholesale Chilean jack mackerel costs roughly one-third as much as Atlantic mackerel.
The Scottish Pelagic Fishermen's Association said there was the potential for confusion, saying "consumers should be able to clearly understand what they are buying".
CEO designate Hannah Fennell said: "If retailers move away from Northeast Atlantic mackerel, they are unfairly punishing the UK industry while instead sourcing a different, less omega-3-rich species from the other side of the world with a significantly higher carbon footprint to the UK market."
The switch follows the so-called "mackerel war", a long-running dispute between the UK, Iceland, Greenland, Norway, the Faroe Islands, the EU and Russia over shared mackerel catch quotas.
The countries have repeatedly failed to agree a unified system for sharing stock and setting catch limits in line with scientific advice.
Mackerel catches in the north-east Atlantic have exceeded the levels advised by scientists by an average of 39% over the past 15 years, according to the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC).
Stocks have plummeted by roughly three-quarters over the past decade, according to the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (Ices).
The intergovernmental body has advised slashing the quantity of north-east Atlantic mackerel caught in 2026 by roughly 70% to allow the stock a chance to recover.
Last year, the Marine Conservation Society said the Atlantic mackerel population was at "breaking point".
The severe depletion of mackerel numbers has led to the fish losing its MSC certification, meaning it no longer complies with many retailers' sustainability policies. Chilean jack mackerel, in contrast, is MSC-certified.
In February, Waitrose said it would suspend sales of fresh, chilled and frozen mackerel due to overfishing concerns, while tinned products would be phased out as existing stock was sold.
The Marine Conservation Society heralded the move as "leading and decisive".
The switch to jack mackerel is being felt beyond the UK, with supermarkets in the Netherlands no longer selling Atlantic mackerel and at least one supermarket in Sweden switching to jack mackerel.

items.title: As luxury stocks slump, is it time to buy M&S or Next shares instead?
items.summary: Shares in companies like the iconic British brand Burberry and LVMH, luxe's most powerful player, have fallen out of vogue, declining further in recent days.
items.body:
As luxury stocks slump, is it time to buy M&S or Next shares instead?
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
The style caravan swings into town this weekend for the glitz and glamour of London Fashion Week.
But behind the smiles and the air-kissing at the designers' shows, fear will stalk the catwalk and Bond Street, home to luxury goods stores.
Shares in companies like the iconic British brand Burberry and LVMH, luxe's most powerful player, have fallen out of vogue, declining further in recent days.
This followed a gloomy report on prospects for the sector from HSBC analyst Anne-Laure Bismuth.
As a consequence of weak sales and disappointing profits at LVMH and other constituents, the STOXX Europe Luxury index is down 20 per cent since January.
Shares in LVMH, which owns ‘houses’ such as Dior, Louis Vuitton, Tiffany and Sephora, have sunk 35 per cent this year to €414.
This is near its lows during the Covid retail shutdown. At the height of the revenge-spending spree that emerged when lockdowns eased, LVMH’s price soared to €841.
Even the seemingly invincible Hermes, maker of the Birkin bag, has tumbled by a third to €1,409.
Burberry is down 17 per cent over the same period – and 50 per cent over the past three years. The company’s fortunes had been reviving, thanks to a new emphasis on 'Britishness'.
Luxury loses lustre: Fashion houses have suffered a slump in recent months
But ‘turnaround’ stocks have been hardest hit, presumably on the belief that the recovery could now stall.
By contrast, shares in high street fashion leaders such as Marks & Spencer, Next and Zara owner – the Spanish giant Inditex – are prospering.
Indeed, so successfully has M&S ‘dumped the frump’ that it will be staging its first-ever show at London Fashion Week, alongside Burberry, Erdem and other elite participants.
Next week, the focus moves to the shows in Milan and then Paris. But the questions British investors will be asking are: should I quit Bond Street for the High Street? Or is Bond Street now a bargain alley?
Why luxe lost its allure
The factors behind the sector’s malaise include the impact of conflict in Iran on Middle East tourism, and the continuing consumer downturn in China, where the passion for baubles and handbags was previously voracious.
Americans may fast be becoming almost as keen, thanks to fortunes made from soaring artificial intelligence (AI) tech stocks. But apprehension over a bubble in these shares persists.
Bank of America analysts say that third-quarter data indicates a dip in demand in the US and other key markets, such as South Korea, where the AI boom has also enriched luxury goods fans.
Yet although an AI stock rout imperils the taste for luxury, the deft deployment of AI could reset luxury goods companies’ relationship with customers, reigniting their urge to spend. Or so argues Claudia D’Arpizio, of management consultancy Bain.
Meanwhile, as Bain also highlights, cost-of-living pressures have curtailed the spending of more than 60 million ‘aspirational’ shoppers worldwide who used to make up about 15 per cent of luxury companies’ clientele.
Some of this pain is self-inflicted. From 2019 onwards, LVMH and the rest raised the prices of bags and other items by 50 to 70 per cent.
Now, as Mamta Valecha, analyst at Quilter Cheviot, points out, LVMH is trying to win back these shoppers.
Initiatives include lipsticks that sell for £120, a more affordable proposition than a Louis Vuitton Neverfull bag, which costs around £1,400 (against £990 in 2020).
Investors can cash in on the catwalk slump as London Fashion Week begins
New Louis Vuitton stores are being designed as ‘immersive brand experiences’ in which a younger crowd can buy lipsticks and dream of one day acquiring a Neverfull.
But Valecha adds that change takes time in a conglomerate the size of LVMH, suggesting that the benefits may not be visible in results for a few quarters.
All this suggests that luxury would not suit risk-averse investors.
But if you want to inject an adventurous twist into your portfolio, it could be worth taking a bet on a bounceback. After all, these businesses have built their reputation on successive reinventions.
Note that Bain still expects growth in the sector of 3 per cent this year and 4 per cent in each of the next three years, while broker Bernstein forecasts 5 per cent.
The Bond Street options
Broker analysts are taking a cautious view, rating the following as a 'hold': Burberry, Kering, the Gucci group and LVMH. But Berenberg, Bernstein, Deutsche and others are more optimistic about Hermes, considering it a ‘buy’ at its current level.
The view of Richemont is also more upbeat, because of this Swiss company's concentration on jewellery through its Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels divisions.
So expensive have handbags become that bracelets and necklaces seem, relatively, affordable, and also a way to hold gold at a nervous geopolitical time.
Rolexes and other timepieces also appear to be seen as a desirable asset – good news for Watches of Switzerland, a British company. Despite a recent retreat, its shares are 38 per cent up this year.
Investors seem to agree with the company’s chief executive David Hurley that ‘your iPhone is going to tell you the time more accurately, but a watch is a symbol of success.’
The high street choices
Shares in Next, the £17.4billion group regarded as the high street bellwether, have bounced by 9 per cent this year to 15,000p. Ahead of half-year results next Thursday, most analysts see the shares as a ‘hold’.
But, on the basis that Next almost always contrives to deliver a pleasant surprise, Citigroup and Deutsche view the shares as a ‘buy’ Citigroup has set a target of 18,400p.
M&S shares have advanced by 76 per cent over the past three years, and by 17 per cent this year to 386p.
But analysts hope for more, with the majority believing M&S to be a ‘buy’ with an average target price of 442p.
The company will be ensuring that the creations that it sends down the runway at its fashion week show support this favourable assessment.
Inditex, the Spanish behemoth and the world’s largest fashion retailer, this week unveiled a 7.6 per cent increase in first-half sales to €19.8billion.
This may have been below forecast but the group has made a strong start in the third quarter, taking catwalk copy specialist Zara upmarket, while expanding its discount chain Lefties. The first store opened this month in Liverpool.
Analysts love Inditex’s strategy, it seems. The shares stand at €54 but are tipped as a ‘buy’ with an average price of €60.
I have stakes in both Bond Street through Burberry and LVMH, and in the high street through Next and M&S. Trends come and go. But diversification is seldom out of style.

items.title: Extra fishy: your tinned mackerel may not be what you think it is
items.summary: Substitution with jack mackerel, a different species, because of dwindling stocks is criticised by consumer group Which? If you’ve recently opened a tin of mackerel and thought there was something fishy going on, you may have been right. An overfishing crisis means that instead of traditional mackerel, some now contain a different fish with a similar name, prompting concerns that shoppers are being short-changed. Over the past year big brands such as Princes, as well as some supermarket own labels, have replaced traditional tinned mackerel fillets with jack mackerel fillets. Continue reading...
items.body:
If you’ve recently opened a tin of mackerel and thought there was something fishy going on, you may have been right. An overfishing crisis means that instead of traditional mackerel, some now contain a different fish with a similar name, prompting concerns that shoppers are being short-changed.
Over the past year big brands such as Princes, as well as some supermarket own labels, have replaced traditional tinned mackerel fillets with jack mackerel fillets.
Although clearly labelled, food experts say jack mackerel is a poor replacement for the oily fish, because it is a different species with a different flavour and different nutritional values. They also say shoppers may not realise a product has changed until they get it home.
The new products are being sold at a similar price despite the fact that it is a much cheaper fish, leading the consumer group Which? to describe it as another example of “skimpflation”.
Tinned fish is an “affordable and convenient way for households to add important nutrients to their diets”, said Sue Davies, the head of food policy at Which?.
“While manufacturers face genuine supply chain pressures and sustainability challenges, they have a responsibility to shoppers to be completely upfront when they change a product’s recipe.
“Skimpflation can feel particularly sneaky as shoppers may not realise a product has changed until they get it home and eat it,” she said.
Lidl is the latest retailer to switch and, in a recent video by the viral canned seafood reviewer Marcus Ansell, he rates its original mackerel fillets eight out of 10 while the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC)-certified replacement scores a lowly 3.5 out of 10.
“Jack mackerel is of significantly lower quality,” said Ansell. “It is quite a bad tinned fish really. I’ve had a lot of messages and some comments on my videos from people who thought they were buying real mackerel and were very disappointed when they tried it.”
Ansell added: “It’s not a substitute at all. . It’s a completely different species and is nothing like mackerel in its taste, texture, or smell … and there’s the health aspect, which is important to some people.”
Compared with traditional mackerel, jack mackerel has roughly half as much omega-3, a fatty acid that it is recommended people have twice a week as part of a healthy balanced diet.
“So they’re scamming us on mackerel now,” said one poster under the review. “Can’t even get some tinned fish without being legged over.”
Chilean jack mackerel costs about a third of the price of Atlantic true mackerel, according to the Financial Times, which first reported the story.
Last year the labelling rules were changed by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs to allow the species to be marketed as “jack mackerel”. Previously it could only be sold as “horse mackerel”, “jack”, “scad” or “trevally”.
The Marine Conservation Society (MCS) warned last year that mackerel stocks were at breaking point owing to overfishing. Its Good Fish Guide, which ranks choices using a traffic-light system, rates north-east Atlantic mackerel “red”, making it a “fish to avoid”.
Princes said it had taken the decision to move its branded range away from north-east Atlantic mackerel following years of concern over unsustainable catch levels.
It added that the “species is clearly identified on our products, and we would consider sourcing north-east Atlantic mackerel again if sustainable management is restored and MSC certification regained”.
Lidl said it was moving its tinned mackerel over to MSC-certified Chilean jack mackerel. “Before our next purchasing window for smoked mackerel, we will review if north-east Atlantic mackerel continues to comply with our sourcing policies and scientific advice.”
Earlier this year Waitrose suspended the sale of mackerel because of overfishing and instead directed its customers to buy herring and other species.

items.title: As High Street heavyweights feel the heat, the message to Labour is clear... do no more harm! ALEX BRUMMER
items.summary: Running retail is never easy with bosses required to cope with fast changing tastes, technological change, and mercurial consumers.
items.body:
As High Street heavyweights feel the heat, the message to Labour is clear... do no more harm! ALEX BRUMMER
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
Running retail is never easy, with bosses required to cope with fast-changing tastes, technological change and mercurial consumers.
Add to the mix successive governments, with little knowledge about how the High Street works, and there is a toxic environment.
Middle Britain favourite John Lewis and no-frills fashion group Primark, in different market segments, are battling these forces.
Both have an advantage over competitors. John Lewis’s partnership structure allows it to be patient about immediate returns as it fights off heavy costs imposed by Labour, ranging from employment bills to energy prices and business rates.
Primark, as part of the Weston family-controlled Associated British Foods Group (ABF), can look through shareholder dissonance.
John Lewis is asking consumers and partners to look through first-half losses and focus on the turnaround at Waitrose, led by its ‘Home of Food Lovers’ shelves, and investment in flagship outlets such as Oxford Street in central London.
Breaking point: High Street retailers are already struggling with a heavy tax burden and higher employment costs ahead of next month's Autumn budget
Spend on tired stores was up 29 per cent, at £246million, in the first half of the year.
There is confidence from chairman Jason Tarry that it can deliver despite the spike in costs and hit to anchor stores from the business rate muddle.
Primark, which aims to separate itself from ABF by the end of 2027, is also in the middle of a critical transition.
Having invested in digital change, in the shape of click-and-collect, it recognises that its Great Britain operations need a full online delivery service.
It has picked up a surplus warehouse and now needs to embrace low-cost
logistics. Market testing suggests that, with each incremental change, sales will improve.
There is a focus on galvanising performance on the Continent, where previous fast growth has gone backwards.
It is also seeking to bring localised success at its Manhattan store in the US to underperforming US regional markets.
This year and next will be years of transition for ABF, where the results will be affected by tricky conditions facing its sugar arm, which has been hit by substantial losses of up to £60million this year and up to £170million in 2026-27.
By the end of next year, there is hope the sugar cycle will have turned, with better returns, and Primark’s swing towards online will have become entrenched.
The interim message from both companies to Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey is: do no more harm.
Public interest
The rate hike to 2.5 per cent from 2.25 per cent by the European Central Bank (ECB) is not a signal that the Federal Reserve and Bank of England will follow suit next week.
The ECB is a special case. Interest rates across the Euroland are lower than in the UK and America, held back, until now, by weak growth and subdued inflation.
Both factors are changing, with signs of an output revival in the EU, despite the Chinese assault on the motor industry, and the threat of rocketing winter gas prices.
Market rates in the UK are already sending out a chill, with both the 10-year and 30-year gilt yields hitting eye-popping levels of 5.37 per cent and 5.93 per cent, respectively.
Consumer price inflation in September is expected to come in higher, fuelled by energy costs.
That trend is not going away, with wholesale gas prices up 128 per cent on the same week in 2025.
A split Monetary Policy Committee has kept its eye on a more subdued labour market. As winter approaches, it will be impossible to ignore runaway fuel, gas and food inflation.
‘Wait and see’ or ‘transitory’, as it was designated in the aftermath of Covid-19 and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, is no longer a prudent option.
In the loop
Elon Musk’s least tech outfit, The Boring Company, is tunnelling the Tesla and SpaceX founder a fresh pot of gold.
A funding round backed by the UAE, California-based Sequoia and others has raised $3billion of capital, placing a value of $23billion on the enterprise.
The plan is to build 93 miles of underground in the Dubai Loop as well as expand a Las Vegas project. Could Musk provide the answer to HS2’s travails?

items.body:
The Range moves from VoCoVo pilot to store wide roll-out: this week's biggest retail technology stories
It's Friday, the weekend is almost upon us, so let’s kick back and reflect on another eventful week for the retail tech space. Here's your briefing on the most important stories from the past few days, including Unity Coffee, Morrisons, Instaleap, Rainbow, Hanshow, Hotel Chocolat, Deliveroo, Mastercard, Primark, DoorDash, and SKIMS.
1. Paul Borrett takes on Technology Advisor role at Unity Coffee following departure from wagamama
Paul Borrett is joining Unity Coffee, a self-service specialist developed by Coffee Nation entrepreneur Scott Martin, as its Technology Advisor. Earlier this year, Borrett announced his departure from wagamama, where he served as Director of Technology. Prior to that, he worked at Costa Coffee.
In a LinkedIn post, Martin said: “If you’ve ever bought a coffee from a Costa Coffee Professional machine, you’ve used something Paul built. He was the architect behind that digital platform - the M2M infrastructure that today keeps tens of thousands of machines connected, transacting and talking to eachother in real-time.”
He added: “I had the privilege of building that vision alongside him the first time round, and I wasn’t about to let the chance to do it again slip by. After a spell at wagamama, and a very short-lived taste of early retirement, I’ve persuaded him back in. Some technical rockstars just aren’t built for the golf course.”
“Paul joins at exactly the point Unity needs him most. We’re not just building a coffee machine - we’re building the intelligence behind it: equipment that flags its own faults before they happen, one data spine running from bean to cup, a machine that adapts its screen and its pricing to who’s in front of it and an app that turns a first sale into a habit. Paul has actually built infrastructure at that scale before and that’s rare, and it’s exactly what this next phase demands.”
2. Paul Stafford goes from client to colleague as he swaps The Very Group for new role at EPAM Systems
Paul Stafford has joined Empathy Lab, an Al native agency launched by EPAM Systems, as Senior Director - Retail Media EMEA. He was previously at The Very Group and has also worked at Superdrug and PepsiCo.
Stafford played an integral role in launching Superdrug’s retail media network Optimo, before joining The Very Group last year to lead its retail media proposition.
In a LinkedIn post, he said: “My retail media journey continues…Last week I joined the Empathy Lab by EPAM team at EPAM Systems as Senior Director - Retail Media Consulting, looking after EMEA. I've gone from client to colleague with one of the sharpest minds in retail nedia, Diana Abebrese, and am looking forward to learning from her and the wider team (and hopefully teaching them a thing or two.”
He added: “I couldn't be more excited to build strategies and solutions for our clients, from revenue generation and media planning through to agentic tooling and orchestration. In the short space of time I've been here I've genuinely been blown away by some of the projects already in flow for so many global retailers, agencies and brands.”
3. Late to the online party Primark announces plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain
This follows the purchase of an automated fulfilment facility in Sheffield. A famous online laggard, the retailer went live with a Click and Collect service in 2022, but owner Associated British Foods (ABF) now says there is "opportunity for profitable growth" through home deliveries.
The move, which was denied following media reports earlier this year, comes as Primark prepares to split from ABF. This is likely to complete in December 2027 and is expected to create two new FTSE 100 companies, with analysts predicting that Primark could be valued at as much as £9 billion, and the food part of the business £4 billion.
“This is a really big day for us here at Primark, with two significant announcements: Our decision to bring home delivery to Great Britain and expanding our franchise business. 
Exciting times ahead,” said Eoin Tonge, CEO at Primark.
A spokesperson for the retailer commented: “Our stores will always be at the heart of Primark. But a lot has changed in online retail in recent years, from how customers shop and their expectations for online delivery. Combined with the digital progress we’ve made, and particularly the success of Click & Collect, we’re confident the time is right to give customers in Great Britain even more choice in how they shop with us.”
Regarding the franchise business news, the spokesperson added: “Building on our partnership with Alshaya Group, we are continuing our growth in the Middle East, expanding into the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. We are also announcing a new strategic partnership with El Puerto de Liverpool that will see Primark enter Mexico for the first time. New ways to shop. New markets. More customers discovering Primark. We’re excited about what comes next.”
3. The Range to roll-out VoCoVo headsets across all 283 locations following one-store trial
VoCoVo has announced a partnership with home, leisure and garden retailer The Range, that will see Series 5 (S5) Pro Headsets and Call Points rolled out across all 283 of its stores. This follows a one-store trial over the course of a year.
The Range colleagues will get instant, hands free communication through the headsets, replacing disruptive loudspeaker calls and reducing the need for them to search the shop floor for one another. The technology will help deliver faster, more responsive customer service by reducing waiting times at tills, service desks and across the shop floor.
Colleagues can contact managers and team members immediately for price and stock checks, quickly coordinate requests and assign tasks in real-time, while two-way Call Points will allow customers to request assistance at the touch of a button and connect with available colleagues.
A Store Manager at The Range says: “The headsets have made a hugely positive impact in-store for both colleagues and customers. Customer service has noticeably improved as queries are answered faster, stock checks are smoother and warehouse to shop floor communication is instant. This has already streamlined Deliveroo and Click & Collect, and I can see the headsets becoming invaluable during patio season. They’ve become essential to daily operations."
“The very impressive results already achieved in our store have laid the groundwork for much bigger savings across the store network. I can’t wait to see colleagues benefitting from the same technology.”
Beth Worrall, CEO at VoCoVo, says: “The initial trial with The Range has shown how they can achieve significant time and cost savings while maintaining outstanding service levels and the optimum in-store experience at the same time. We’re looking forward to working alongside the team to implement the technology across all its stores.”
5. Chinese retailer Rainbow opens its first Hanshow powered Store Digital Twin supermarket in Shenzhen
Rainbow, a Chinese omnichannel retailer, has opened its upgraded Shahe sp@ce supermarket in Shenzhen. Developed in collaboration with Hanshow and Rainbow's technology subsidiary Lingzhi Digital Technology, the project marks its first Store Digital Twin implementation, bringing together real-time store visibility, decision support and operational execution within a live retail environment.
Located in Shenzhen's Nanshan District, the Shahe sp@ce location has served the local community for nearly 17 years. In 2026, the wider Shahe Rainbow development was upgraded into an urban lifestyle destination that brings together retail, dining, services and entertainment. The move reflects Rainbow's broader ambition to expand the role of physical retail beyond transactions and create a more engaging destination for the surrounding community.
The newly opened sp@ce supermarket, built around Rainbow's "City • Garden • Food Hall" concept, features nine experiential areas designed around different food, lifestyle and community occasions. The store also incorporates Rainbow's intelligent fulfilment centre, supporting more efficient home delivery services and aiming to strengthen the connection between in-store shopping and its broader omnichannel retail model.
As its first Store Digital Twin enabled supermarket, the store brings together more than 17,000 IoT devices and AI capabilities to provide greater visibility into store conditions and support more timely operational decisions and actions.
6. Morrisons teams with Instacart owned Instaleap to boost online marketplace and in-store fulfilment
Instaleap, a company providing software for e‑commerce fulfillment and last mile operations that was recently bought by Instacart, and Morrisons have announced a new partnership.
“We’re proud to partner with Morrisons, one of the UK’s most respected grocery retailers, as they continue to strengthen their omnichannel offering,” says Antonio Nunes, Head of Instaleap. "Consumers now increasingly expect ordering from their local supermarket to be as easy as ordering take-away. Meeting that demand at scale - efficiently, reliably - takes technology built specifically for grocery. That's exactly what we're giving Morrisons."
“We’re constantly looking for ways to make online grocery shopping easier and more convenient,” says Charlotte Exell, Group Online Director at Morrisons. “More of our customers are choosing to shop from us through one of our immediacy partners and they expect an efficient, dependable service every time. Working with Instaleap powers our online operations behind the scenes, helping us deliver fresh groceries directly to our customers’ doors quickly and reliably.”
7. Firsts for both DoorDash and SKIMS as they shake hands on rapid delivery service across US stores
DoorDash and SKIMS have announced a new partnership to offer on-demand delivery from all of the latter’s retail stores across the US. DoorDash is SKIMS’ first on-demand delivery partner, and SKIMS is the first brand on DoorDash to offer a selection spanning undergarments, everyday clothing, and outerwear.
"We were built on one idea: you should be able to get everything you need in your neighbourhood, right now. And increasingly, that's not just dinner, it's what you're wearing to dinner too,” says Shanna Prevé, Chief Revenue Officer at DoorDash. “SKIMS has built an iconic brand that’s become part of so many people’s everyday wardrobes, and that’s exactly what we want to your doorstep. We're proud to be SKIMS' first ever on-demand delivery partner, giving people a completely new way to shop a brand they already love."
SKIMS was co-founded in 2019 by Kim Kardashian and Jens Grede.
“Our focus has always been on understanding what our customers need and finding better ways to serve them,” says Robert Norton, Chief Commercial Officer. “Our partnership with DoorDash gives customers greater flexibility and convenience when shopping SKIMS, making it easier to access the products they want, when they want them. It’s about putting the customer at the centre of the experience and providing a solution that works for them.’’
SKIMS is available on DoorDash from 17 stores across 11 states and Washington, D.C., with nine additional stores coming soon to the platform.
8. CVS Health's Vivek Misra joins RTIH Innovation Awards judging panel for 2026 edition
We're hugely pleased to announce the addition of Vivek Misra, Lead Director - Engineering, CVS Health to the judging panel for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards. In this role, Vivek heads up technical strategy and digital platform transformation for major consumer businesses, including FrontStore, Photo, and OTC Health Solutions.
He specialises in large scale web architecture and cloud native commerce platforms, advancing AI native and agentic technologies to elevate the customer experience. He is also an active contributor to the technology community, serving as a judge for innovation competitions and technology programmes, including InnovateQA, Technovation, and as a co-author and peer reviewer of research publications focused on emerging technologies, AI, and intelligent QA automation.
Welcome onboard, Vivek!
Further information on our judging panel can be found here. In addition to Vivek, it includes representatives from JD Sports Fashion, Holland & Barrett, Walmart, Amazon, Boots, C&C Group, Warner Bros. Discovery, East of England Co-op, PoundFun, Austen & Blake, and Gordon Ramsay Restaurants.
9. Hotel Chocolat agrees exclusive tie up that brings retailer on to Deliveroo quick commerce platform
Hotel Chocolat has announced an exclusive partnership with Deliveroo, launching initially with five of its locations - Manchester Cross Street, Chiswick, Staines, St James's and Wimbledon. Customers will be able to shop the Velvetiser, Hotel Chocolat's new boxed selections, its signature selectors, and Velvetised Creams.
Carrie Martin, UK General Manager at Hotel Chocolat, says: “Thoughtful gifting has always been at the heart of what we do, and we're constantly looking at how we can make it easier for customers to mark the moments that matter.”
“Partnering with Deliveroo gives customers a completely new way to access and send Hotel Chocolat gifts: combining the quality and originality they expect from us with greater choice and flexibility. It’s an exciting next step in how we’re growing the brand and meeting customers where they want to shop.”
Suzy McClintock, VP Consumer at Deliveroo, says: “We are building a new destination for gifting at Deliveroo. Customers are no longer using our platform just to shop for themselves but to send something special to a loved one, whether for Valentine’s Day, Christmas, a birthday and more. As a true gifting specialist, Hotel Chocolat brings real brand authority and category expertise to our retail offer, and we are excited to help them reach more consumers who are on a mission to find a meaningful last minute gift.”
10. Mastercard unveils Payeux Tapestry in London and agentic AI research predicting £370 billion spend by 2030
One in ten consumers will routinely use artificial intelligence to shop and pay by 2030, according to a report published by Mastercard that surveyed 26,000 people across Europe and canvassed the opinions of four futurologists. The report was unveiled in London this week and forecasts AI driven consumer spending will hit £370 billion a year globally by the end of the decade.
Carried out in June and July this year in conjunction with Opinium who questioned 13,000 teens and 13,00 parents in pairs across 13 European nations from France and Germany to Italy, Spain, and the UK, the research showed 18% of teens already use an AI assistant, such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, once a week to help them compare products before purchasing. This compares to 9% for the parental adults surveyed.
A third of the surveyed teens said they would happily hand over control to a fully AI run shopping assistant that chooses and pays for products. Speaking at a press event to launch the research, Agnes Woolrich, SVP MasterCard UK, commented: "AI has transformational potential."
"Businesses will have to think differently," she argued, in an exclusive chat with RTIH, who were in attendance at the event prior to the research’s wider general release on 8th September. Woolrich added: "Investments in retailers’ brand, loyalty programmes, and in machine readable digital estates will all be essential in the future, as agentic AI adoption advances."
“I expect the technology to follow the classic adoption curve with early adopters right through to laggards evident. This goes for consumers and merchants," she said, while also unveiling a new artwork commissioned to accompany the report that apes the famous Bayreux Tapestry.

There are now just three weeks left to get your submissions in for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
The entry deadline for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards is fast approaching. The big day is Friday, 2nd October. That’s just three weeks away, so don’t delay, start working on your submissions today!
The awards, sponsored by 3D Cloud, Business France, and Retail Technology Show 2027, celebrate global tech innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world. Our latest winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC (Prince Consort Rooms) in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
Further information on our judging panel can be found here. The panel includes representatives from JD Sports Fashion, Holland & Barrett, Walmart, Amazon, CVS Health, Boots, C&C Group, Warner Bros. Discovery, East of England Co-op, PoundFun, Austen & Blake, and Gordon Ramsay Restaurants.
Click here for FAQs, categories, and information on our judging panel.
Sign up for an account and submit your entry or entries here.
Key dates for 2026
Friday, 20th February: Awards open for entries
Friday, 2nd October: Awards entry deadline
Tuesday, 6th October: 2026 finalists revealed
Wednesday, 7th October - 20th October: Judging days
Wednesday, 4th November: Winners announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC (Prince Consort Rooms) in Central London.

Is there a fee to enter the awards?: It is free to enter and you can do so across multiple categories.
Do I need to complete all the sections in the entry form? No, but the more information you provide, the better chance you have of producing a successful submission.
Is there a certain timeframe for nominated projects, initiatives etc? Yes, nominated projects, initiatives etc should have been completed (or substantially completed) during the last 12 months.
Who has visibility of our completed entry form and what information will be public should we win or be shortlisted? Only our Editor, Scott Thompson, and judging panel will view submissions. The information provided in the summary section of the entry form will be made public.

Shortlisted companies will be invited to attend an event at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November (consisting of a drinks reception, three course meal and awards ceremony).

items.body:
Aldi UK completes transition to SAP ERP system as final batch of discount retailer’s Irish stores go live
Aldi UK reports completion of a SAP ERP system deployment across its store network. In a LinkedIn post, Nathan Loftus, National Supply Chain Director at Aldi UK, said: “And just like that.. The last 2.5 years working on transitioning Aldi UK across to the SAP ERP system is complete.”
He added: “From our first PO raised back in February 2024, to our final batch of Irish stores going live this week, it’s been a huge effort and a massive congratulations to all involved across the business.”
Responding to the post, Aldi UK’s Karolina Blaszczyk commented: “A huge milestone, congratulations to everyone involved! Having experienced the transition from an operational perspective, it’s clear how much work has gone into adapting processes while continuing to keep stock moving and stores supported. A massive collective effort across the business!”
Shop & Go
Earlier this year, we reported that Aldi UK was binning its checkout-free stores trial and converting its only Shop & Go location to a standard Aldi Local with self-service.
The store in Greenwich, South East London went live in 2022 at a time when checkout-free stores were being touted by many industry observers as the next big thing in retail. But the technology never really took off in the UK, with high profile failures including Amazon ditching its ambitious Just Walk Out technology powered Amazon Fresh experiment, just four years after the US online giant launched its first grocery store in London.
An Aldi spokesperson said: “Whilst our Shop & Go trial has now come to an end as planned, our Greenwich High Road store will remain open as an Aldi Local, ensuring customers can still get everything they need at unbeatable Aldi prices.”
Changing times
Last year, Aldi said it was making changes to Shop & Go, moving from a tap in to a hybrid experience.
In a LinkedIn post, Lennart Hoffmann, Lead Engineer Seamless Stores at Aldi DX, said: “Since opening our first checkout-free Shop & Go store in London in 2022, we have continuously evolved the customer experience to make shopping faster, easier, and more convenient. After introducing tap in during December 2023, we are excited to announce the next big step in our journey: Shop & Go is going hybrid.”
He added: “Our new hybrid store model puts customer choice at the forefront - keeping the ease of checkout-free shopping while bringing the concept closer to the traditional Aldi shopping experience.”
As with any other Aldi store, customers could just walk in. At the exit, they could choose how they wanted to pay: use the retailer’s app or tap on a fast lane, or try new self-checkout terminals. These let people manually scan their items or use an AiFi powered checkout system.
Hoffmann added: “This evolution reflects our commitment to understanding and responding to the needs of our customers. We’re offering more flexibility to suit different shopping preferences while maintaining speed and convenience. We’re proud of this milestone and look forward to welcoming customers to the new Shop & Go experience.”
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
Physical stores will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards are now open for entries and celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world.
Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
Check out our 2025 winners here.
Our 2025 hall of fame entrants were revealed during a sold out event which took place at The HAC on 16th October and consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, and awards ceremony presided over by award winning comedian, actress and writer Tiff Stevenson.
In his welcome speech, Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor, RTIH, said: “This is the awards’ fifth year as a physical event. We started off with just 30 people at the South Place Hotel not far from here, then moved to London Bridge Hotel, then The Barbican, and last year RIBA’s HQ in the West End.”
“But I’m conscious of the fact that, to quote the legend that is Taylor Swift, You’re only as hot as your last hit, baby. So, this year we’ve moved to our biggest venue yet, and also pulled in our largest number of entries to date and broken attendance records.”
He added: “This year’s submissions have without doubt been our best yet. To quote one of the judges: The examples of innovative developments across both traditional and digital retail spaces were truly remarkable.”
Congratulations to our winners, and a big thank you to our sponsors, judging panel, the legend that is Tiff Stevenson, and all those who attended our 2025 gathering.

Skechers has selected KNAPP as technology partner for what is pitched as one of Europe’s largest fashion and footwear automated logistics projects, with a footprint of around 230,000 m² (2,475,699 sq ft) and a planned capacity of more than 3.3 million storage locations.
Opening in stages that will be complete by mid-2030, the logistics centre in Liège, Belgium will start to supply the European market from a single location at the close of 2028 and will be designed to allow future growth. The facility will handle up to ten million pairs of shoes per month.
An existing European distribution centre (EDC) in Milmort in the province of Liège is reaching its capacity limits. “For more than 23 years, Skechers has placed its trust in Wallonia as a strategic base for its European operations - and this new phase is the next chapter of our growth,” says David Weinberg, COO at Skechers. “This massive, automated and sustainable building puts us at the forefront of distribution to Europe and makes us fit for the future.”
KNAPP is implementing an integrated process that handles all material flows from goods-in to goods-out in a single solution. At its heart is one of the largest Evo Shuttle systems in the world, which stores Skechers’ cartons across more than three million storage locations. Also included is a shuttle system for replenishment and buffering, as well as goods-to-person workstations, an automatic pallet storage system and extensive conveyor and sorting systems. All processes are interlinked thanks to the KiSoft software suite by KNAPP.
“This next-generation logistics centre was developed in close collaboration with Skechers’ teams and represents a huge technological milestone,” says Oliver Lehner, Vice President Partner & Products Solutions at KNAPP. “The solution combines a high degree of integration and performance to efficiently handle large volumes and provide excellent service to end customers.”
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
Supply chain automation will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards are now open for entries and celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world.
Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
Check out our 2025 winners here.
Our 2025 hall of fame entrants were revealed during a sold out event which took place at The HAC on 16th October and consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, and awards ceremony presided over by award winning comedian, actress and writer Tiff Stevenson.
In his welcome speech, Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor, RTIH, said: “This is the awards’ fifth year as a physical event. We started off with just 30 people at the South Place Hotel not far from here, then moved to London Bridge Hotel, then The Barbican, and last year RIBA’s HQ in the West End.”
“But I’m conscious of the fact that, to quote the legend that is Taylor Swift, You’re only as hot as your last hit, baby. So, this year we’ve moved to our biggest venue yet, and also pulled in our largest number of entries to date and broken attendance records.”
He added: “This year’s submissions have without doubt been our best yet. To quote one of the judges: The examples of innovative developments across both traditional and digital retail spaces were truly remarkable.”
Congratulations to our winners, and a big thank you to our sponsors, judging panel, the legend that is Tiff Stevenson, and all those who attended our 2025 gathering.
Editor and Founder of Retail Technology Innovation Hub

items.summary: Iceland will become the first British high street brand to open a shop in the Falklands.
items.body:
Now Iceland sets its sights on the Falklands! Frozen food chain to become first British high street staple to open a store on islands
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
Iceland is set to become the first British High Street brand to open a shop in the Falklands.
The frozen food retailer will open the new supermarket in the islands' capital Stanley in early December.
It comes just days after Argentine president Javier Milei reopened the row over the ownership of the islands and vowed to 'recover' the territory.
Iceland boss Richard Walker, who is known for campaigning on retail crime, said: 'We are proud to be backing Britain by becoming the first UK high street retailer to open in the Falkland Islands. The Falklands are a special part of the British family and it's always been an ambition of mine to support it.'
He added that the opening will mark an 'important moment for the business' and its 'international aspirations'.
Iceland has 960 stores in the UK and around 40 internationally. It holds around 2.3 per cent of the UK grocery market.
Lord Walker added: 'I will personally be visiting the Falklands to officially open the store and I'm looking forward to welcoming our new customers through the door.'
Iceland is set to become the first British High Street brand to open a shop in the Falklands
The shop is being launched in partnership with local retailer Keller Stores.
Iceland said the shop will sell its own-label frozen products as well as brands including My Protein, Cathedral City and TGI Fridays.
It comes as Argentina's president reiterated claims for sovereignty and stated that Britain is a country 'on a path of decline'.
Mr Milei argued there are 'multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved'.
Unlike Britain, he said that 'Argentina's future, however, is flourishing and will prevail'.
He has pledged to hit oil companies drilling in the territory with sanctions as well as filing criminal charges against Israeli energy firm Navitas Petroleum for operating in its waters.
In a televised address, Mr Milei said: 'The Falklands are Argentinian. Historically and legally. There can be no argument. They are part of the Argentine territory.
'The islanders on their usurped territory do not have a legitimate right to self-determination and any argument on any such self-determination is invalid.'
In response, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband wrote: 'The Islands are British and will remain so because that is the overwhelming position of the islanders.'
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the UK's commitment to the territory was 'absolute and unshakeable'.
Lord Walker is known for speaking out against the worrying levels of shoplifting and abusive incidents against shop workers in the UK.
He has recently proposed allowing trained security staff in shops to carry equipment such as truncheons and pepper spray.
